utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours, and good morning. MR. JOHN RALSTON, recalled.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, when we left off on Friday, you were testifying about the conditions in the detention facilities that were run by the Bosnian Serb authorities. Let me stay on that subject for a moment and ask you whether high ranking members of the SDS, that is, close associates of Dr. Karadzic, visited these detention facilities while these inhumane acts were taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. As stated previously, detention of civilians in various facilities followed the political and military takeover by the Bosnian Serbs. The Office of the Prosecutor has evidence to establish that the SDS, the military and the police were formally involved in the operation of the facilities. The existence and operation of these facilities was known to civilian and military leaders of the Bosnian Serbs. Further, lines of communication within the SDS and the army was such that this information regarding the facilities passed to Karadzic and Mladic. Mrs. Plavsic in late May/June 1992 acknowledged to a senior United Nations military observer that camps existed for prisoners of war on the Serb side, but she alleged that similar camps were maintained by the presidency and Croat forces. The Officer attempted to visit these camps on the urging of both parties, but both parties equally frustrated his attempts to visit the camps. There is also evidence that various high ranking SDS members had knowledge of and visited the detention facilities when the inhumane acts which I have described occurred. Velibor Ostojic, Vojislav Maksimovic and Petko Cancar in Foca and Ratko Dukic in Vlasenica each were involved in the SDS at the Republic level. Witness testimonies indicate that each of these officials were well aware of occurrences at detention facilities in their regions. Ostojic was seen at the Livade detention facility. Miro Stanic, Head of the Crisis Staff and President of the SDS in Foca for a period of time in 1992, had his officer in Velecevo women's prison. Dragan Cancar, a relative of Petko Cancar, was a Commander of Livade facility. Major Radmilo Zeljaja, a Commander of the Prijedor Corps, visited the Omarska camp with a delegation of Serbs from Banja Luka and Prijedor in July 1992. Major Slobodan Kuruzovic, in addition to being a military officer, was a member of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor and the Commander of the Trnopolje camp. Simo Drljaca, Prijedor Chief of Police, was seen on a regular basis in Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje detention facilities. Additionally, he played an important role in the negotiations with police in Kozarac and Ljubija in relation to the signing of an oath of allegiance to the Serbs and in the surrendering of civilians after the Serbian attack on Kozarac. Simo Miskovic, Commander of the Crisis Staff and President of the SDS Prijedor, was seen by a number of witnesses in the Omarska and Keraterm camps during their operation between May and August 1992. Srdjo Srdic, President of the Red Cross in Prijedor and an SDS deputy in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and later in Republika Srpska, was also seen in Omarska and Keraterm camps during their operation.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, was Dr. Karadzic ever asked about the camps and conditions in those camps and has he ever expressed an opinion about the camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic has been asked repeatedly about the camps. He has denied that abuse took place in the camps and continues to deny wrong doing in the camps. In an interview in the Der Spiegel magazine in May 1995, Karadzic pointed out that "The camps were not for civilians ... they were exclusively for POWs", prisoners of war. As late as February 1996, Karadzic in a reported interview, denied that his army set up detention camps across Bosnia in which tens of thousands of Muslims were imprisoned, tortured or killed. He said that this was Muslim propaganda".

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, are you familiar with the Thompson Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Could you explain to the court what it was and what its purpose was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I refer to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: If you would refer then to Exhibit 61?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Thompson Commission was set up under the auspices of the Council for co-operation and security in Europe. It is ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt, prosecuting counsel. When you are talking about Exhibit 61, is that something that is available for the Judges, or is that something that is in the case file? What is the status of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It should be in the binder that I provided the court, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Commission I referred to is referred to in the report as an humanitarian mission which was headed by Sir John Thompson of the United Kingdom. The main task of the mission was to survey the human rights situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina through direct observation of the detention camps and centres throughout the country in so far as it could in the one week duration of mission. The team saw places of detention where thousands were held often under conditions of severe hardship and sometimes of terror.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: When did the Thompson Commission perform its survey, Mr. Ralston?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was from 29th August 1992 to 4th September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please read directly from the report some of their significant findings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On page 6 of the report under the heading "Lack of respect for Civilian Population: The mission determined that a complete range of individuals, both males and females, young and old, are now being held throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina in various places of detention. We met with prisoners as young as 17 or even less, and as old as 83. "The crucial point is that thousands are being held against their will, or under conditions which make their departure from the place of their confinement virtually impossible. Legally speaking, the people held in places of detention of various natures fall into three categories: "(A) Prisoners of war. These prisoners have taken an active part in hostilities and can be legally detained as combatants under the Third Geneva Convention of 1949. The Mission saw very few of these. It was our impression that much of the fighting was to the death. "(B) People who allegedly had been hiding weapons in their homes and/or possessed information of potential military significance. Their civilian non-combatant status should have protected them from military detention although they could, arguably, be subject to judicial proceedings. There were probably a significant number of these. "(C) People who were taken prisoner because they lived or worked in the zone of combat. These people were not taking part in hostilities but were seen as enemies due to their ethnic origin. Their civilian non-combatant status should have protected them from detention. This category was easily the largest. "Our experience suggests that a comparatively small percentage of prisoners are genuine POWs. The remainder should never have been imprisoned. We are not impressed by claims that they were incarcerated in their own safety or simply because they happened to be resident in a combat zone. "It is impossible to escape the conclusion that most prisoners are innocent people who have been seized as hostages to promote ethnic cleansing. They are pawns in a vicious game played by nationalist politicians. These innocent people should be released forthwith". On page 8 of the report they go to the responsibility of the leaders, I quote: "Despite the existence of war lords, the bulk of the evidence points to the responsibility of acknowledged leaders. The Mission believes that, in general, leaders exercise effective control over their military and civilian structures. Contrary to what is usually accepted, the so-called uncontrolled elements are marginal. They exist, but their importance has been exaggerated by various leaders who find them a convenient explanation for numerous barbarities. "The Mission has seen camps well organised with military personnel or policemen doing what they were told to do. There is no reason for the international community to condone implicitly or otherwise any departures from the agreements signed in London or Geneva. "The existence of the 22 May agreement shows that all parties have from an early stage been aware of their obligations and have claimed to carry them out. At least some Serb authorities have stated that they observed the provisions of Mr. Karadzic's order of 19th August 1992 which sets out additional obligations. "However, the mission is very conscious that on all sides there have been numerous breaches of the Geneva Conventions and that to a significant extent some of these continue. The most widespread breach by all parties is the long continued detention, in some cases of more than three months, of civilians who cannot possibly be classified as prisoners of war. The largest number of these appear to be in Serb places of detention and, therefore, while the international community should bear down heavily on all parties, it should do so particularly firmly on the Serbs".

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ralston. Now let me ask you with regard to some of the persons who the Office of the Prosecutor has previously indicted for committing serious violations of International Humanitarian Law in these camps, particularly Meakic, Nikolic Jelisic and their subordinates, to your knowledge, Mr. Ralston, have these people been arrested or punished for the crimes which they have committed in these camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, they have not been arrested and punished.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn briefly to another subject area, Mr. Ralston, and that is the issue of the appropriation of property. In the course of your testimony on Friday, you touched upon that topic and I would like to touch upon it again briefly. Could you please explain to the court the process of how property was appropriated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The various manners in which property was appropriated, one that I have referred to previously is the seizing of property from the civilians as they were taken to detention facilities. Another significant manner was when people, driven through fear and harassment, moved to leave their municipalities, they were forced to obtain permission to do so through the Crisis Staff, often having to pay large sums of money to facilitate their movement from the area. In addition, they were required to sign a document stating they were leaving of their own free will and stating that they were handing over all of their property to the officials of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, do you have a sample of one of those voluntary change or surrender of property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: That is Exhibit No. 62; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, could you please read the English translation of that document into the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is headed "Republika Srpske, Mrkonjic Grad, reference 018021/92. Mrkonjic Grad, 14 October 1992. Statement about voluntary change of residence. I", the citizen is named, "resident of Mrkonjic Grad, on behalf of my immediate family", the members of his family are named, "declare that we decided of our own will without any pressure to change our place of residence. By this statement we agree that our movable and immovable property is left to the competent authorities of Mrkonjic Grad municipality. By expressing my own will and the will of my family, I personally undersign this statement. This statement serves as permission for the Municipal Assembly of Mrkonjic Grad issued to above mentioned persons so that they can freely leave the territory of Mrkonjic Grad municipality". Statement given by, signature, submitted to, person who gave the statement, to Municipal Assembly, Mrkonjic Grad. There is an official seal on the document. The official seal is worded "Republika Srpska, Municipal Assembly of Mrkonjic Grad, Executive Council." There is a footer on the document "Municipal Assembly of Mrkonjic Grad".

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, throughout Friday's testimony you summarised a systematic pattern of conduct that took place in municipalities where non-Serbs formed the majority population. That pattern included the establishment of camps, deportations, murder, appropriation of property, sexual assault and the like. What has been the effect of this conduct in these particular municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can go through some of the municipalities I have referred to. For example, in Foca there were approximately 21,000 non-Serbs in 1991; by August 1993 there were only nine. In Bosanski Samac there were approximately 17,000 non-Serbs; by July '95, 98 per cent had gone. In Vlasenica, the majority of non-Serbs had been expelled. In Brcko, from 79 per cent of the population, or approximately 69,000 non-Serbs, the overwhelming majority who were not killed or detained left by any means possible. From Prijedor, of approximately 64,000 non-Serbs, by June 1993, 88 per cent had gone. By July 1993, the majority of non-Serbs had been expelled. In Kotor Varos, there were 36,670 non-Serbs in 1991. There are few left. In Zvornik, there were around 35,000 non-Serbs expelled from that municipality. In Bratunac, approximately 20,000 or 92 per cent of non-Serbs were forced into exile. Rogatica municipalities, of approximately 12,000 non-Serb inhabitants, 2,700 were forced to flee to Gorazde, 3,700 to Sarajevo, 1200 to Zenica and about 2,500 were forced to move to Zepa before being expelled from that area in 1995. Visegrad, 13,500 non-Serbs have been totally removed from the area. In addition, the non-Serb population of Srebrenica and Zepa, which included many non-Serbs who fled there from other areas, have been expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, let me refer you to Exhibit No. 63 and ask you to explain it to the court. It will be set up for you in just a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You will recall from my testimony on Friday I pointed out that these areas, in the areas occupied by the Bosnian Serbs, the shaded areas were areas where the non-Serb population was in a majority as of the 1991 census. The areas that I have just given you the population details about show that, as a result of their activities, we have a totally Serb dominated population status in all of these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, I would like to turn your attention to another subject now and that is the knowledge of Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic with regard to their obligations under International Humanitarian Law. Specifically focusing on General Mladic, what does our evidence show in relation to his knowledge of obligations under the Geneva Conventions and normal customs of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have evidence to indicate that it is standard JNA military training to include education on the obligations of the Geneva Convention and other conventions in relation to war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Was Dr. Karadzic likewise aware of relevant legal standards that applied in armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: In that regard, Mr. Ralston, let me refer you, please, to Exhibits 64, 65 and 66, and ask you to identify each of those exhibits and explain their significance to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 64 is a document which is a declaration which was signed, I think it was, in November, on November 5th 1991. It is a statement on respect of humanitarian principles. It sets out: "We, the undersigned, undertake to respect and ensure respect of International Humanitarian Law and remind all fighting units of their obligations to apply to the following fundamental principles". It included provisions that, "All detaining authorities must ensure the protection of prisoners in the civilian population and civilian property must not be attacked". This declaration was made by the Presidents of the six republics in The Hague, the six republics of the SFRY. Exhibit No. 65 is an agreement on the release and transfer of prisoners. I am sorry, I have the wrong document here.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Why do you not turn to Exhibit 66 then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit No. 66, which was signed on 27th August 1992, it is an agreement which was signed by Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Izetbegovic identifying, "The agreement is a programme of actions on humanitarian issues agreed between the co-chairman of the conference and the parties to the conflict on 27th August". The agreement includes at point 3(4): "All practices involving forcible displacement or forms of harassment, humiliation or intimidation, confiscation and destruction of property and all acts involved in the practice of ethnic cleansing are abhorrent and should cease forthwith".

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, we will turn to another area. Exhibit 65, your Honour, should be an exhibit dated May 22nd 1992 in which representatives of Dr. Karadzic agreed in an ICRC agreement to reiterating respect for human rights and ensuring that humanitarian law would be abided by. Mr. Ralston, in addition to those agreements, were Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic actually notified of violations of International Humanitarian Law that occurred or were occurring in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have an example of this type of direct notification to them and in that regard would you please turn to Exhibit No. 67?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit No. 67 is a document addressed to General Mladic on 2nd March 1993 from the European Community Military Monitoring Headquarters. It raises issues such as the deteriorating situation in the Muslim pockets of Eastern Bosnia; reports about the exodus of 3,000 from Trebinje and setting out their reason to conclude that these people did not leave their homes voluntarily. It refers to Muslims, 1500 Muslims, being expelled from Sipovo and being forced to cross the front line at Turbe, amongst other things.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, did the United Nations and the Security Council issue resolutions and statements regarding violations of International Humanitarian Law that were occurring in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Were Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic aware of these resolutions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, I would like to turn to Part III of the indictment which is that part of the indictment describing a offences in relation to UN hostages and their use as human shields. Can you tell me when UN peacekeepers were taken hostage in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of four separate occasions when UN peacekeepers or military monitors were taken hostages; firstly, on 13th April 1994, secondly, on or about 21st November 1994, again on or about 26th May 1995 and, finally, in July '95 in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe each of those incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On 13th April 1994, after NATO attacks on Bosnian-Serb army military targets following shelling of Gorazde, throughout Bosnian Serb held areas United Nations military observers and Canbat soldiers were either apprehended or subjected to restrictions on the freedom of their movement. This action was taken by the Bosnian Serb army. On 21st November 1994 there was a NATO air strike at 13.05 against Udbina airfield in response to shelling of the Bihac pocket by Croatian Serb forces. On November 23, 1994, there were NATO attacks against Bosnian Serb army surface to air missile sites in the area of Otoko and Dvor. Following this there was an almost complete block of movement on all UNPROFOR personnel, especially around Sarajevo. In sector South West 55 members of CanBat were detained by the Bosnian Serb army Ilijas Brigade at six locations around Visoko and Breza. All Bosnian Serb army checkpoints in the area of responsibility were closed to UN traffic. The Bosnian Serb army ordered all United Nations military observers to be confined to their quarters. Following the NATO air strikes of 25 and 26 May 1995, Bosnian Serb military personnel captured or otherwise detained a total of 284 UN military observers and UN peacekeepers in Pale, Sarajevo, Gorazde and other locations, and held them as human shields and hostages in order to prevent further air strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: In relation to Srebrenica, were UN peacekeepers taken as hostages, Mr. Ralston?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Approximately 55 Dutch UN peacekeepers were taken as hostages during the attack by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: That was in July 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please focus your attention to the seizure of UN military observers and peacekeepers by the Bosnian Serb army in May 1995 and explain to the court what happened in that particular series of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. UN military observers were dispatched throughout the Sarajevo area, according to areas of responsibility, and were supposed to check that heavy weaponry would not be used by the Bosnian Serb army nor by the Bosnian army. The main means to accomplish their duties was to make regular patrols and have contacts with the two armies. The UNMOs were not armed. After seizing UNMOs in the Pale area, Bosnian Serb military personnel selected certain military observers who had been taken as hostages to use as "human shields". There were 35 military observers detained from eight teams. From on or about 26th May through 27th May 1995, Bosnian Serb military personnel physically secured or otherwise held these UNMOs against their will at potential NATO air targets, and near previous impact sites including the ammunition bunkers at Jahorinkski Potok, the Jahorina radar site and a nearby communications centre in order to render these locations immune from further air strikes. The military observers were detained in various circumstances. Some were handcuffed or otherwise physically retained, and used as human shields at potential NATO air strike targets, while others were under different restrictions, in their accommodation or elsewhere. Bosnian Serb military personnel held the UN peacekeepers throughout their captivity by force or threat of force. In some instances, the UN hostages were assaulted. During and after protected negotiations with the Bosnian Serb leaders, the hostages were released in four ways between 3rd and 18th June 1995. Peacekeepers, not only UNMOs, but also a significant number of UNPROFOR infantrymen, were subjected to detention by Bosnian Serb forces. These soldiers had been posted to a number of checkpoints around the Gorazde and Serb-held suburban areas of Sarajevo in late May 1995. Within hours or even days of the air strikes, each of their checkpoints was captured by the Bosnian Serb military or military police, under force or serious threat of force. All detainees were transported to various locations in Bosnian Serb held territory, where they were held for periods of time up to approximately 18 days.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, did the taking of these United Nations military observers and peacekeepers appear to be widespread and systematic throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Let me refer you to Exhibit No. 69. It will be shown on the elmo; once it is, I would ask you to explain what it means to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you see marked on this map, the squares show the locations where either military observers or peacekeepers were taken from. You will note that the localities cover the whole of the area controlled by the Bosnian Serbs at that time, and there is an example in each of the areas under each of the separate Corps commands that I have detailed evidence of earlier. The inset which shows the locations in and around Sarajevo or the Sarajevo opstina where military observers and peacekeepers were taken from.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Were Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic informed that taking UN peacekeepers as hostage was a violation of International Humanitarian Law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Senior UN officials protested such actions. In addition, following the May '95 hostage taking/human shields episode, there was widespread public outrage at the practice. This outrage was conveyed to both Karadzic and Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: What were their reactions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In general terms, their response was that the hostages were being held as hostage against further NATO attacks. They stated that the lives of the hostages were in NATO's hands. An example of Dr. Karadzic's attitude is contained in an interview published on 29th August 1994 in the Der Spiegel magazine. The Der Spiegel interviewer asks: "How do you then assess the proposal by US President Clinton to lift the arms embargo against the Muslims and to thus arm your military opponents?" Karadzic is reported to have stated: "If the arms embargo is lifted, we will not adhere to one single resolution of the UN Security Council any more. Then we will take Blue Helmet troops hostage, we will shoot down innumerable planes, and we will arrest all foreigners on our territory. We will really do everything that is to the advantage of our people without any consideration for anyone". In a 17th May interview with Der Spiegel, Dr. Karadzic is reported to have said: "If NATO were to attack, they would be taken hostages, if they were to attack, they would be our enemy". With respect to General Mladic in a 30th May 1995 article in The International Herald Tribune, he is quoted as follows: "General Ratko Mladic, the Bosnian Serb Commander, said he had stopped chaining hostages to potential targets as human shields against NATO air attack, an act that had prompted worldwide outrage. But he warned that the soldiers would continue to be exposed at the sites, including an ammunition dump and a radar base until the UN backed down".

utterances.speaker: MR.  HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, I would like turn now to another topic and that is the lack of cooperation by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in securing the arrests of Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic. Your Honour, we have filed with this court a report describing our efforts to secure the execution of arrest warrants. That report is a matter of record with this court. We have in addition to that requested that the Registrar transmit to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and to the Republika Srpska publication for newspapers notifying both of the accused of the indictments. The warrants have not been executed in either the Republika Srpska or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; nor have the advertisements notifying both of the accused that there are indictments for them in The Hague, they have not been published in either the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or in the Republika Srpska. (To the witness): Mr. Ralston, since Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic have been indicted, have either or both of them been in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are numerous reports that both of them have been in Belgrade, and I will take you through those reports. General Mladic is reported to have met with President Milosevic and the Chief of General staff of the Yugoslav Army, General Momcilo Perisic in Belgrade on 3rd August 1995. Dr. Karadzic is reported to have met with leaders of the FRY in Belgrade on 29th August 1995. Both Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic are reported to have been in Belgrade for talks on 14th September 1995. General Mladic is reported to have been checked into a hospital several days before 19th September 1995. Dr. Karadzic is reported to have arrived in Belgrade on 25th September 1995 for consultations before the New York meeting between Milan Milutinovic, Muhamed Sacirbegovic and Mate Granic. On 19th October 1995, a delegation, including Dr. Karadzic, is reported to have met an FRY delegation at Dobanovici near Belgrade for talks. On 29th November 1995, the leaderships of the FRY and Republika Srpska, including Karadzic, are reported to have met in Belgrade. On 7th February 1996, Dr. Karadzic is reported to have held talks in Belgrade with Mr. Milosevic, discussing the new situation that emerged after the arrest of General Djorde Dukic Dukic. General Mladic is photographed in Belgrade attending the funeral of General Dukic on 21st May 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes the evidence to be presented through Mr. Ralston. We would tender now a single volume of exhibits that we have discussed in the course of this hearing. If the court has any questions of Mr. Ralston, he is available to answer those questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have taken note of the file and have accepted your statement as such and it has been noted down by the Registrar. Do you have any questions which you would like to ask to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Have you finished your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have finished our presentation, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I now turn towards my colleagues: Judge Odio-Benito, do you have any questions you wish to ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Just a clarification. In connection with Exhibit 29, I do not remember if we saw the clip 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We presented those video clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Clip 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Clip 4, we did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: So are you going to show it or you deleted it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We deleted it, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: JUDGE RIAD (In translation): Mr. Ralston, you mentioned, and I quote you, "High ranking SDS members visited the detention facilities and were well aware of the atrocities committed". You also mentioned that Crisis Staff and President of SDS Prijedor and others were seen in the Omarska camp and in other camps". Could you explain to us the relationship between the SDS, the Crisis Staff and General Mladic and Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff were set up by the SDS officials in each of the municipalities. The Crisis Staff was responsible for the overall co-ordination of what happened in each of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did they receive orders from Mladic or were there any signs of collaboration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given the close co-operation between the military and the police officials in each of the takeovers, it appears to me that, yes, there was direct corroboration -- collaboration between the military and the SDS Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So, in your assessment, they cannot act without the knowledge or the consent of General Mladic or Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You also mentioned that when interviewed Dr. Karadzic denied that the camps detention facilities were not for civilians, but they were for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he make any statement or did he deny also the practice of atrocities and torture in the camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he has. He has been interviewed many times in relation to the camps by various members of the media. In general, he has denied the atrocities. As early as August 1992 he was interviewed, and I recall one particular interview where he denied atrocities (and he was being interviewed in relation to the Prijedor camps), he denied that atrocities had taken place and further went on to say that if anything had taken place, he would punish the people responsible. However, there is clear evidence that the people responsible have not been punished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ralston.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, I have two questions or perhaps three I would like to put to you. You described -- do you hear me -- for the court the procedure and the methods which were used for the ethnic cleansing taking place by the SDS. You expressed, I think, on Friday the similarities between the one camp and the other camp, the separation, the segregation, men, women, etc.. My question is, did you find any written references or written instructions for this procedure that was similar in its methods and was contemporaneous in time? Did you find any written memos, any written instructions, which described the procedure which took place in several camps at more or less the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were numerous reports as to the existence of such a document, and I in fact have had a witness describe it to me, but I have not personally seen a document of that nature.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As reaction, I would like to know from the Prosecutor, have you looked for any sources, are you looking for any written documentation, or all the documents you have, do you feel that they are sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, our investigation is ongoing. We continue to investigate each of the allegations and each of the offences described in this indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I know that we are talking about Rule 61. We want to confirm an indictment and, therefore, I would like to hear that answer, that there is an ongoing investigation, and I think it is an opportune memo to say so. My second question to Mr. Ralston, as regards the Mission of humanitarian organisation, the Red Cross mission, sometimes there were written and visual documentations. Were these missions prepared well in advance and do you have any sources indicating to you how they were received? Did they tell the prisoners what to say? Did they threaten the prisoners if they did not say what they were told to say, so that they would not have too serious repercussions on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we have discovered evidence along those lines. For example, in the Batkovic camp, which was regularly visited by the Red Cross, I have been told by witnesses that the elderly and the young were removed from the camp before the Red Cross arrived, taken to another location and then ferried back to the camp at night once the Red Cross had gone. I am also aware, particularly in relation to the visits to the Omarska camp, that prior to the international community attending that camp, the majority of the prisoners had been removed. I think it was about 180 of the fittest looking prisoners were selected to remain at the camp for these visits. I have also been told that prior to visits, the prisoners were warned about talking to the people who were visiting and what they should say. I think in the film clip we showed on Friday afternoon, where the journalists were attempting to the speak to the inmates at Omarska facility, it can be seen that they are very reluctant to talk to the people who were visiting the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. My third question, Mr. Ralston: Do you have any documentation, any witness statements, any sources, written or verbal, of the indictment of Mladic and Karadzic after 1992, so between '92 and 1995? I know that this morning you have shown us the authority that they had in the negotiations at the international level. That is one thing. I would like to know whether after all these offences this acquisition of territory, the ethnic cleansing which was taking place with a certain degree of efficiency, what was the role of these two individuals? Do we have witnesses on their attitudes, on their speeches where they congratulate the actors? Do we have any conferences where they were present? Do we have any information, because we have the impression that after 1992 we see these two leaders in international conferences, but we do not have, it seems to me, any understanding of their role from that moment onwards. Do you have any sources and are you keeping it for the procedure for the future if at any stage there will be a cross-examination of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I can assist you there. We have conducted numerous interviews with various senior officials in relation to the role of both Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic and their relationship. I think it can be summarised in two to three points: (1) that Dr. Karadzic was the political leader and the supreme commander of the military; (2) General Mladic was the senior military officer in the Bosnian Serb army and responsible for its actions; (3) by way of example, we have a media clip where Dr. Karadzic is reported as promoting various members of the military after the fall of Srebrenica for their activities in that particular action.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I just want to add something to that. The Chamber is really wondering that there must have been meetings of the Serbs from 1992 to 1995, so there must have been some information made by the Minister of Defence, by Dr. Karadzic. Do you have any minutes of those sessions? There was an official journal. I suppose, there must have been an agenda. If Mr. Ralston is not in a position to answer, perhaps the Prosecution could answer or we could ask your Office to answer that question perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. At this point in time, as you have pointed out, the purpose of a Rule 61 hearing that we have taken it in the spirit is not to present all of the evidence available to the Office of the Prosecutor. We do that for reasons that are to us quite obvious. We believe that our burden in the course of a Rule 61 hearing is to present evidence sufficient to show your Honours that we have a reasonable belief that Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic have committed the crimes that are alleged in this indictment. We have specifically not presented other evidence because of reasons of security and otherwise.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a last question I would like to put. (To the witness): At the end of your statement, I think in order to show us the inadequacies of those who are protecting the suspects, is it confidential or secret if I would ask you if your office has had top level contact with Pale or Belgrade in addition to the publication in the newspapers which we know because that after all started this initial hearing, but in your office have you had any contacts since the indictment at a high level so that you have told the people in Belgrade or in Pale of our intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this is probably covered by confidentiality, but I think you could tell the Tribunal that contact has taken place and they have led to the decision of the Prosecution to do something about it, so that they respond to the requests of this court. Thank you. I think there are no further questions. I think we can thank Mr. Ralston for his statements and wish him everything of the best in his future mission with the Office of the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, we now want to call our next witness -- if you want to have a recess or something before that, I do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think it might be a good idea that we have a break between the two witnesses before starting the next witness. So, we will adjourn now and start at 11.20. (11.05 a.m.) (The court adjourned for a short time) (11.20 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We shall resume the hearing. Please be seated. Prosecuting counsel, please have the next witness brought in?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. We call Mr. Jan Van Hecke. MR. JAN VAN HECKE, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Van Hecke, first you have to put on the head sets and see if you can hear me all right. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Now you should be given a version of declaration you might read out for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Van Hecke. Please be seated. You have been called before the International Criminal Tribunal as a witness by the Office of the Prosecutor. Prosecutor, you have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Would you please state your name and even spell it for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Jan Van Hecke, that is, J-A-N V-A-N H-E-C-K-E. I am an investigator with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, for your information, this examination will deal with the shelling and sniping of Sarajevo and also briefly touch on the shelling of Tuzla. We have prepared some exhibits we are going to introduce to you. I would now ask the usher maybe to give these three binders containing the picture and things we are going to introduce. These binders contain also something pertaining to the next two coming witnesses. There is something in the binders to separate them from what we are going to deal with now. (To the witness): Mr. Van Hecke, you stated that you are a member of the Office of the Prosecutor. How long have you been in that post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have been in this post since April 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you tell us of your previous occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I am a Belgian police officer and I have been that for 18 years, and I currently hold the rank of Detective Commissaris in the Judicial Police in Belgium, and from 1988 until I joined the Office of the Prosecutor I was the head of homicide and drugs investigations in the area of Leuven in Belgium.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. What kinds of investigations have you been working on since joining our office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have been part of a team investigating allegations of war crimes against the civilian population of Sarajevo. Focusing principally on allegations of sniping and shelling attacks on civilians. These allegations cover the period from April/May 1992 when armed hostilities commenced in Sarajevo to the Dayton Accord in December 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How many cases would that involve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we established at the start that it was impossible fully to investigate every allegation of sniping and shelling over that period. So we, therefore, have had to select a sample of cases from the total. We investigated between 60 and 70 sniping and 38 shelling cases.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the methods used in doing these kinds of investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, our basic method has been to obtain the investigation files of the Sarajevo authorities who investigated a very large number of incidents. The foundation for investigations was not as readily available in 1992 by comparison to the evidence subsequently gathered by the Bosnian authorities. From their files, we have located and interviewed victims, eyewitnesses and relevant corroborating witnesses and also the investigators, principally those who carried out forensic and ballistic investigations. The methods and conclusions of those experts we have put to independent artillery and ballistics experts for opinion and confirmation of the quality of the forensic conclusions of the Bosnian investigators. In many instances officially produced and certified medical documents and death certificates have been obtained in respect of the wounded and/or killed victims. In every case we investigated we established that the incidents involved civilian or non-combatant witnesses and victims, and that there was no military activity by Bosnian government forces at the relevant place and time. We have also been obtaining evidence regarding the disposition of the respective forces around the city and the chain of command of the Bosnian Serb forces or VRS during what has become known as the Siege of Sarajevo. Essentially, the same Bosnian Serb Corps remained to conduct the siege for its duration. This was the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, as it became known. Formerly, this Corps, already based in the area prior to the outbreak of hostilities, was the 2nd Military District/4th Corps of the Yugoslav National Army, the JNA. Remaining troops of this Corps formed the base of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and took over the weapons of the former JNA unit. This included some tanks and a large amount of artillery which was already sited around Sarajevo when the armed conflict began.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now ask you to describe the geography of the area and give some description of the city. In doing so, your Honours, I would now introduce Exhibit No. 71 which is an aerial photo taken out of a issue of the National Geographic Magazine and shows the city. You can even see from which angle you look at the city. I will now ask Mr. Van Hecke to describe what we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, as you probably know, Sarajevo is the capital city of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the seat of national government. Historically, the city goes back to Roman times and through the ages it has been a major cultural and commercial city in the region. The 1991 census in the city, I am told, recorded a population of about 526,500 people. The ethnic composition of that time was 49.35 Muslim, 29.9 Serb, 6.6 Croat and 10.7 Yugoslav with 3.5 described as "other" groups. Can I have the -----

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You now have it on your monitor -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you see, the city occupies a long narrow valley on the banks of the Miljacka River and is dominated by steep surrounding mountain slopes looking down on the city. Sarajevo runs from east to west -- Sarajevo runs from east to west along the river and extending up the slopes with a densely built up residential and commercial centre and the "old town" to the east and then spreading westwards to residential and commercial developments in a number of newer municipalities on open ground at the western end of the valley. You will see that through the naked eye the city lies in a "bowl" and it is clearly seen in detail from all sides from the hills.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Would you now like to insert the video or would you go on with this one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we have also two photos as exhibits to show Sarajevo from the hills, Exhibits 72 and 73, so maybe we can first show these before we go over to the video?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, please. Exhibit 72 and 73?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So you have a clear view on the city from the hills. The next one, please. So that is about the same as the previous exhibit, so I think we can now insert the video as Exhibit 70.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: 70, yes, please. When it starts, will you then comment on it for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will. So when the hostilities commenced in April 92, the forces which were to become the Republika Srpska army occupied the surrounding hills and confrontation lines were quickly established around the city. They have remained substantially unchanged throughout the conflict. From these positions uphill, the VRS had a commanding view of the city and its people. These forces had -- you see here in the picture -- large stocks of both light and heavy artillery and ammunition to turn on the city, and from about May '92 Sarajevo has, effectively, remained under siege and been subjected to shelling and sniping. You can see from these hills how they had an overview of Sarajevo. You can stop the video, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. We now may turn to Exhibit 74 which is the map showing confrontation lines without armaments. Will you please comment on that when it appears on your screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can show the confrontation lines from this map prepared from UN sources, which clearly shows how the city and, therefore, its civilian population were trapped in the "bowl". From these positions all around Sarajevo, the VRS made deliberate attacks on the civilian population without military objectives or justification over and above any legitimate military action on the lines. So you see the red line on the map is a confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: It remained the same all through the period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It remained basically the same throughout the period, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You told us initially that you have been investigating sniping and shelling incidents. Would you now tell us about this sniping activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can give an overview of the sniping and I can say that the sniping campaign had been conducted throughout the siege and civilian casualties have included young children and elderly of both sexes. So the campaign has affected a wide number of locations in the city and has been sustained throughout the siege to a greater or lesser degree. Basically, the population could never feel safe in certain parts of Sarajevo, even when indoors in their homes. Certain sniper positions targeted civilian residences and apartment blocks and people have been killed and wounded sitting on their own couch, asleep or performing basic chores. The sniping attacks involved the use of direct fire weapons. This means that the target is selected and deliberately visually targeted. The weapons are directly aimed to the person. So maybe we can show .....

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, we can present now Exhibit No. 75 which contains a photo of sniping weapons. You will, please, go on and explain to the court what kind of weapon that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see here three examples of sniping weapons. You will see that these weapons include rifles and automatic small arms, usually fitted with a powerful optical sight. In the case of the campaign against Sarajevo, sniper weapons have included light machine guns and what you see, what you see down here ---

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The one at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the one at the bottom, yes, that is M84 or NSV heavy machine gun. This weapon has a range up to 2,000 metres and is fitted with a powerful optical sight for accurate targeting and is commonly referred to by the local people as a "Death Sower", as it is accurate, powerful and can fire bursts of rounds. The local knowledge of the attackers and their commanding views of the city streets from their vantage points on the hills and in the high rise buildings enabled the snipers accurately to select and target their victims. In many places, the confrontation lines placed the sniper close to civilian areas, for instance, Grbavica -- I want to go back eventually to Exhibit 74 to show you. So you see Grbavica here where the confrontation line is running through the city at the border of the Miljacka River; there were snipers from there targeting the main roads going through Sarajevo from the high rise blocks on the Bosnian Serb side, and this was called, this main road, famous "sniper alley".

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about what form or what way this sniper campaign took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, a number of streets in the city were a source of constant danger. I have myself seen a number of improvised barricades erected to afford some shelter and protection in the city and the suburbs, such as we have Dobrinja here in the west of the city, where the people were very exposed in wide areas between apartment blocks. You see the confrontation line on both sides of Dobrinja. Old damaged buses and other vehicles and containers were widely used for these barricades. We can eventually show these, some of those barricades, in Exhibit 76.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, please. 76?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, you see, old cars placed here as a barricade to give shelter for the sniping so people could run behind this, let us say, wall of vehicles that could protect them from sniping from the other side. Exhibit 77 is another example. You see here at the end the buses that were placed as sniping protection. Exhibit 78, please. You see again buses that are placed to protect people. Exhibit 80, that is UN anti-sniping position. So they placed themselves often on places where there was a lot of sniping to try to avoid people being sniped there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: To block a street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To block the street, yes. A number of locations became well known as "sniper nests" and certain streets or crossroads where there was the greatest danger became known as the "sniper alleys". Civilians on the streets or in their homes even were often targeted and were victims. However, and that was one of the main problems, civilians were forced to take risks exposing themselves to snipers in order to perform the basic necessities of life such as fetching water, food and whatever. We investigated cases where people were shot in their own homes and shelters and crowded buses and trams, it was often a target of snipers, and what occurs, of course, inevitable civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you identify some typical patterns that this sniping activity took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To an extent, yes, I can. At some locations it was a regular occurrence with periods of intense fire; on other occasions or in other places, it could be more random. Sometimes there would be bursts of shooting and breaks. The people would come out in a hope they would be safe for a while in a break and the snipers would then open fire again to catch them out. Even during cease-fire snipers would break the agreement and civilians would get killed. It happened often that people who wanted to help a victim could not reach that victim because of continued sniping, or that they tried to reach the victim and because of that they became a victim themselves. There were also examples of victims who could have survived but died because nobody could reach them to help them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you give some examples of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, most of -- there are a lot of examples already in the indictment, so I will not repeat every little piece of the indictment, but you can be sure that a lot of fatal sniping included children from two, three years, elderly people, women. So, clearly, the sniper could clearly identify his victim and target it deliberately on civilian people, even children, elderly people, women, whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The distance was not greater than that they could see it through this optical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Optical, oh, no, the distance was sometimes only a couple of hundred metres. When I showed you before the confrontation lines at Grbavica, there were four high buildings in Grbavica on the Bosnian Serb side, and from there they had a clear view of the people walking in the street or running in the streets. With their optical devices, they could easily take out their victim and there was no mistake possible who they were targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you know from the reading of the indictment which we listened to initially in this hearing, lists of people were given to you, children starting with a boy age two, going on with 15 children, then there was a list of female from the age 20 to 50, over 50 years old, then there were elderly, a list of 20 persons, females in the ages of 60 and 70 years and of females and males in a mixture. (To the witness): In your opinion, when you have been doing these investigations, were these people listed in the indictment targeted individually and hit individually by these snipers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Without any doubt it was clear that they were civilian people and they were targeted by the snipers. They could very well see who they were targeting.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you give the court an estimated amount of people killed by sniping fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is very difficult to say, but in our investigations we included 37 people who were killed in sniping and 83 were injured. Of course, this is only a very small sample of the total amount of people that were killed or injured by sniping fire.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you cannot come closer than that? That is your estimation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our estimation will be at least hundreds.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: At least hundreds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least hundreds, but I do not have the right statistics with me to be closer than that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are turning from the sniping to the shelling. I will ask you now to start with telling us what kinds of weapons were used for the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were three kinds of weapons used for the shelling, that means guns, howitzers and mortars. I think we can show Exhibit 81.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: 81, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But maybe before we go further with 81, I have a video clip prepared too about sniping, so before we go over to the shelling maybe we can first include that video about sniping?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 70 too.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: 70 again, please. (Exhibit 70 was shown)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have the film on my screen. You can see how the victims try to take shelter and crawl away. Here we can see how people had to cross a street sometimes between barricades or places that were especially exposed to sniping and, as you can see, these people are all civilians. Here you see a woman who was hit by a sniper bullet. Like I said before, people had to come out for their basic necessities. That is an example of a sniper injury. So, you see, it is only a video tape of a couple of minutes, but in Sarajevo this went on for 44 months in a row during the whole siege.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: We went into the area of the shelling. Did shelling and sniping take place simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it went on through the whole period of the siege of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 44 months.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When they were shelling there was also sniping fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course there was. That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you now tell us something about the weapons used for the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will go back to Exhibit 81. So Exhibit 81 shows us the mortars that were used around Sarajevo. We have the 60 millimetre mortar, the 82 and the 120 millimetre. Exhibit 82 will show us other weapons that were used, again howitzers. So you have starting the 76 millimetre mountain gun, 105 millimetre howitzers, the 152 howitzer gun, M84. All these weapons were used around Sarajevo, to target Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. You may also tell us about where these weapons were placed in relation to the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then we will have to go to the map on Exhibit 83. So this is basically the same map as we have seen before, but this time with the weaponry deployed around Sarajevo. In the left-hand top corner you will see how to interpret this map with the weapons deployed around Sarajevo. So the green is artillery, pieces of artillery, batteries. You have the mortar pieces and batteries, anti-aircraft weapons and the yellow crosses are tanks around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: There is a key in the ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a key in the left ----

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: -- left upper corner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. So, as you see, there was a lot of artillery around Sarajevo. The heavy article was withdrawn in 1994 under the exclusion zone; an agreement which left mainly mortar batteries on sites around the city. The mortars continued to be widely used, many being fired on preset co-ordinates from base-plates in fixed locations. This would provide a consistency in target area and a number were on fixed locations targeted on civilian areas in the city, meaning they were fired time and again on those areas.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what the exclusion zone agreement was all about and when it happened exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happened in February '94 when the heavy artillery had to be withdrawn from Sarajevo to a distance of 20 millimetres from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Due to an agreement ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: -- between the parties. You have already told us about the weapons used and now we see where they were deployed. Do you want to make a description of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you a bit more about the weapons. It is going to be a little bit more technical, but basically there were these three types of weapons or the guns, howitzers and mortars. Guns fire a high velocity shell from a rifle barrel, making the shell spin and giving it a higher range and accuracy. Guns can fire on a flatter trajectory and be used for direct targeting. Howitzers fire large shells on a high trajectory and are used for air bombardment and suppression by way of indirect fire. So it is capable to fire over a hill or buildings on to unseen targets. Then the mortar operates in a similar way as the howitzer, firing a shell also on a high trajectory. In the case of a 120 millimetres mortar shell, it can fly to up to 6.5 kilometres high. It can take 45 seconds before the target is reached. These weapons were also used for the same, for area suppression. The shell explodes with a wide area of fragmentation. The whole shell casing disintegrates into hundreds of pieces of hot jagged metal with considerable killing and wounding potential. A 120 millimetre shell can have a killing radius of 54 metres and a danger area of 500 metres. So it very wide. Mortars are principally in normal warfare intended to pin down troop movements on open ground, but within the confines of city streets and buildings, these weapons have a devastating effect and can inflict heavy casualties. The accuracy of mortars is affected by a number of factors, including the meteorological conditions, of course, at the various heights of the trajectory, the wind speed and direction of the wind and even the effects of the weapon's base-pate, of the "bedding in" of the base-plates when it is fired. The VRS had a number of mortars on fixed "bedded in" plates with settings pre-aimed at the city.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: VRS is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: VRS is the Bosnian Serb army, yes. This allowed for a higher degree of accuracy than normally achieved by mortars, because within the base-plate is "bedded in", you have a bit more stable plate to fire from. The Bosnian Serb army used their mortars around Sarajevo often in a very special way. In normal warfare, a mortar is used from a position from where you can see the target, like I explained before, so it is an indirect weapon normally. But around Sarajevo there were mortar positions where the gunner clearly could see the target into the city. So, we can maybe go through and run through rather fast through a lot of exhibits because I will come later on back to the exhibits I will show now. So, starting with Exhibit 84, please? This is state hospital so you see that even hospitals were shelled. The next one, please? Here we have a view on Kosovo Hospital where you see the impact of an artillery shell. 86, please? Here is another view on Kosovo Hospital, so also hospitals were often target of shelling. 87, please? In this street on the left-hand side was a shelling on 28th August '95. So on the left-hand side, the yellow building is a closed market of Sarajevo. I will come later in time back to these specific files. Next one, please? Here in the middle of the picture you see the crater created by the 120 millimetre mortar shell that landed there. You will see also the bullet all around the place. The next one, please? Can I have the next one, please? Here you see the same place from another angle. Next one, please?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And what we see is also blood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is blood, yes. Here you see the result of this shelling, one of the results of this shelling, where 43 people were killed. Here you see how a foot was cut off of a victim. The next one, please? That is part of a hand you see laying in the corner there; so that when investigators came on the site they often found rest of human bodies after the victims were taken to the hospital, to the morgue. The next one, please? These are also victims in the morgue. As you can see, there are women among them. The next one, please? This is a water line that was shelled in Dobrinja in 1993, so you can see all the canisters laying at the left side of the road.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: These white things are buckets, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor counsel, could we turn down the lights just a little bit because it is hard for us to really to see this clearly on our screens? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here you see another mortar impact in Vase Miskina Street, one of the pedestrian streets in the city of Sarajevo, where a bread line was shelled in the early days of the war in May, 27th May 1992. The next one, please? That is one of the victims of this shelling, a little child. The next one, please? That is another victim of this shelling, a woman. Can I have the next one, please? This one is a shelling that happened in January '94. Children were sledging in this residential of area of Alipasino Polje in the west of Sarajevo when three mortar shells landed in the neighbourhood of these children. Can I have the next one, please? Here you see a footstep in the snow and blot around the footstep. The next one, please? Here you have one of the sledges of the children who were victims of this shelling. Could I have the next one, please? This is another site in Dobrinja where people in February '94 were waiting and queuing for humanitarian aid. You see the mortar impact here. The next one, please? You will see some of the victims of the shelling, so I think we can go through with the photos. The next one? It is another victim clearly in civilian clothes. The next one, please? That is a young woman also killed in this shelling. The next one, please? Another woman killed. The next one? That is man killed in the same shelling. The next one? It is another man killed. The next one, please? That is another woman who was killed. Next one -- as you have already seen on the previous photos, they were people from all ages, all sexes, who were victims of this shelling. Here you see a man on his way to a water pump. The next one, please? Here you can imagine how people were queuing to have water at the water pump, so it was a real gathering of people when they had to go for water and these places were often deliberately shelled by the Bosnian Serb army. Can I have the next one, please? This is Simon Boliva Elementary School in Dobrinja. You see it, the second photo, the photo at the bottom. The water pump was placed in the school. People used to come there to get water and were queuing there to get water and this place was shelled in June '95. Can I have the next one, please?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is Dobrinja a suburb to Sarajevo or part of the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If you want, we can maybe go back here to Exhibit 74, to the map of Sarajevo? So you see Dobrinja here in the south west of Sarajevo. So it was almost a pocket in the siege. West and east from Dobrinja were the Bosnian Serb forces. Can we go back to the previous exhibit, please? So that on the top photo you can see where the shell hit the wall at a height of about four metres. It hit a wall there and on the bottom photo you see the stabilizer of the shell that fell on the other side of wall. In fact, it is a place that is shown by an arrow on the top photo where the shell landed. Can I have the next one? So you see on these photos also the buckets and everything that were standing around this water pump. People were lining up there that day to get water. The next one, please? At the bottom photo you see already a victim, an elderly man. The couple of next photos we will see are also victims of this shelling. Next one, please? These photos will show you that, in fact, shell exploded at a height of a couple of metres so you will see that all these people have wounds in their heads. Next one, please? So you will see how these fragments of this shell, what these fragments can do to people. The next one, please? This is a woman who was killed in the same shelling. The next one? That is also one of the victims. Like you see, all have injuries at their heads. Next one, please? Yes. I will have to present a lot of horrible photos, but it is only a small part of what happened in Sarajevo during this three and a half years. The next one, please? This is a shelling of another water line that we have seen a photo before already when we saw all the cannisters at the left side. This is taken from another angle with some of the bodies still laying on the site. The next one, please? This is the same situation as you saw before. When you see the effect, the explosion of the shell has also on things like glass around the side where it exploded. I think this was it for these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. You now have shown us the result of the shellings and you have shown us the weapons used for the shellings. My question to you now is whether other specific weapons were used besides from those you have already shown us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, our investigations revealed that in 1995, on a number of occasions, modified air bombs were deployed. Significantly, a number were launched in the direction of the TV building in Sarajevo and always fired over Bosnian held areas. I think this is significant because these weapons hit a number of apartment blocks and other civilian buildings, and they were basically inaccurate weapons, unsuitable for any precision attack on a military target. I will show it again on Exhibit 74, if you want to show it?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you find 74 for us? There we are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, the first air bombs were launched from this area, firing in this direction -- I am not very good at drawing, but I will try to do my best -- firing in this area, so you see it went all the way over Bosnian government held territory. Then one air bomb was launched from this area, of course out of the confrontation line, and fired in this direction, so it went all the way also over Bosnian government held territory. The majority of the air bombs were launched from the western side of Sarajevo and went into this easterly direction. So these bombs were very unreliable and inaccurate, so they could fall and explode at almost every point of its trajectory, so I think that is why they were fired in these directions.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you have any pictures of them so we can see what they look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have a couple of pictures exhibit and also some results of what happened after an explosion of an air bomb. So if you can give me Exhibit 135, please? So here you see a drawing of an improvised air bomb. So the front part is the actual bomb.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Designed orginally to be used to be dropped from an aeroplane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This was a standard 250 kilo bomb, and these are designed to be dropped from an aeroplane to which the Bosnian Serb strapped four 102 or 128 rocket motors and fitted a time fuse in a parachute. The weapon was fired from an angled rail mounted on a truck. These weapons have been really described as inherently inaccurate and indiscriminate. With motors strapped to the casing, the balance of the projectile is uncertain and the rocket engines could burn at different rates and power. There is no guiding system at all or means of control after firing. Accordingly, the weapons are unpredictable for a variety of reasons. Experts have stated that they are unsuitable for specific military targets where you need an accurate hit. Accordingly, they would appear to serve purposes of random targeting and random damage with the consequent fear it creates to the civilian population. So we can maybe go to the next exhibit? Here you see parts of such bomb that was found back on one of the sites where it exploded. The next photo will show you the sites of an explosion where these parts were found. The next one, please? So you will see what damage such a bomb can cause. That is the house where the bomb landed and there wee in total 12 houses very severely damaged in this explosion. Can I have the next one, please? Here you see a photo of the woman that was killed in an explosion of this air bomb, a woman who lived in the house that you saw previous. Can I have the next one, please. This is a site around an apartment block where an air bomb landed when exploded again in Alipasino Polje, you remember of the sledging children, the same residential area. Can I have the next one? You will see the air bomb exploded in this apartment building taking away a couple of stores. The next one, please. This is one of the victims of this air bomb explosion. It is a woman. The next one, please? Here you see another victim of this air bomb. So people are really mutilated by these bombs. The next one, please.
