This is another boy killed by an air bomb, by fragments of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Should we dim the light a bit? It would make it easier to see these things or can you clearly see them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I have the next one, please? This projectile is -- people told me that this was a gravity bomb. It was found in Ilijas with the closure of the surroundings of Sarajevo. Can I have the next one, please? You see a number of these projectiles. Can I have the next one, please? Here you have even a clearer view on the projectile. Can I have the next one, please? Here you can see a photo of the rocket engines without the air bomb itself, so without a 250 kilo bomb. So you see the plates down on the picture. That is where the bomb was attached to the four rocket motors. Can I have the next one, please? Here you have a view from the back of the engines and, to give you a clear view how big it is, the man who took the photo put a box on it. So this motor are generally 122 or 128 rocket motors. Can I have the next one, please? OK, that was it, I think, for the air bombs.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Were the investigators able to determine what types of weaponry that were used at different times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The basic ballistics test you normally do is a crater analysis on site. But, initially by the shrapnel marks on the target, the degree of penetration into the target and the fragments of shell, investigators could determine the nature and calibre of the weapon and shell. Every type of shell has its own characteristic details. You could compare it eventually with the tyre of a car, when you can see the difference between a Goodyear and a Michelin. Other physical features at the point of impact then enable a crater analysis to be done, otherwise the testimony of eyewitnesses give further details to complete the picture.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were these types of crater analyses done in each case of hits on the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in almost each case we had the results of the Bosnian ballistics experts and sometimes UN teams also carried out crater analyses. We have had independent experts check the methods and results and in some instances I too have visited the sites and checked the fact alongside the Bosnian investigators.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you could determine the type of weapon or could you also determine the direction of the fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes of course. The experts I have spoken to say that, in reality, when you do a crater analysis, it is accurate in between one or two degrees. They always take a margin of plus or minus five degrees to be on the safe side. I think this is pretty accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Just to go back to the use of air bombs, is there any account kept of how many air bombs were dropped on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we have done investigations on 16.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the range from which these bombs and the shells were fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is one of the things you normally cannot reveal from crater analysis. One of the things you investigate when you do a crater analysis is taking the measurements of the angle of decent, so the angle in which the shell came down. When you have determined which shell was used and what the angle of descent was, with a mortar using the shells that were used in the conflict, you have seven levels of propellant charge and along the line of the direction of fire you can plot the points relative to the quantity of charge used. So you have, in fact, seven areas, because a mortar shell is normally delivered with six additional charges and the charge can be clipped on the tail of the shell. There is nothing on the ground or amongst fragments to indicate what charge level was used in a given case. However, these weapons make a very loud noise when fired and, accordingly, if fired close by witnesses would hear the shot and the shell explode. If they did not (which I found to be usual), then it indicated the shot was fired from longer range than rather from shorter range. A complete investigation goes further than a strictly technical investigation, and witnesses are very important. So we have seen both civilian witnesses, UN witnesses and UN military to determine the origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: OK. You told us about these crater analyses. Can you give us some examples of the shelling case you have investigated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to talk a bit more of this crater analysis ---

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I visited shelling impact sites in Sarajevo and I followed crater analysis exercise on site, so I can show some exhibits of crater analysis and after that I will give a more technical explanation. The technical explanation will be short on a number of ways to conduct crater analysis because they were not that often used, and I will go deeper into the "Main Axis" method which was the method that was almost every time used in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we can show first Exhibit 122, please? So here you see ---

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you lower the lights again, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- here you see a crater goes by a mortar impact alongside. We can show how long the crater is. Can I have the next one, please? Here you can see a stake in the tunnel. This is what they called the "Fused Tunnel" method. I will come to that a bit later when I give the technical explanation. But I first prefer to explain the main methods of crater analysis that was used, so we start with Exhibit No. 124, please. So this is a crater analysis done another time because it was already done shortly after the impact by Canadian investigators, but as an exercise we did it over again. You see that technicians from the police first with the liquid tried to clean the crater. The next one, please? Here the technician is with a broom sweeping the liquid away to get traces more clear. Can I have the next one, please? So here you can see that the traces are already more clear. The next one, please? Then they put police car close to the crater and one of the policemen will stand on top of the police car to take photos of everything that happens during the crater analysis. The next one, please? The next thing that the technician will do is mark all the traces on the crater with chalk. We can go to the next one. The man continues on marking it with chalk. Go to the next one, please? Here you see what we have after the technician marked all the traces with the chalk. You see most of the traces are on this side and smaller traces on the other side of the crater. From the centre of the crater, he put two sticks alongside the bigger traces, what is called these big traces, the paw or the rose, you take the two sticks and they form a certain angle. When you take the middle of that angle, that is why it is called Main Axis method, you put a stake there and that stake is in the direction of fire. After determined the middle of this angle, you put on a compass on the crater itself and you can see from which direction the shell had been fired.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You said something that where the accuracy of one to two degrees on the compass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, because mortar gives a specific trace like you see, and the middle of that main axis of these traces is the direction of fire. The next one, please? That is about the same as the previous with another zoom. The next one, please? You can see on this photo too that they mark here the north, so the north of the wind rose. Can I have the next one, please? You can see here that a map of Sarajevo and surroundings is placed in the direction of fire and, of course, put right in the right direction, and with compass then is determined from which side the shell came. The next one, please? Here people are cleaning up everything. So that was it for these exhibits. So I will maybe give now a little more technical explanation of the other matters too?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we have to see that crater analysis is part of the overall investigation and visual evidence, for example, seeing the flash of gunfire, the sound and any observed time of flight of the shell can all help. Crater analysis follows certain methods for certain types of shells. For artillery pieces and shells with quick fuses, the "Fuse Furrow and Centre of Crater" method requires a stake to be placed in the furrow made by the fuse to the front of the shell crater and another in the centre of the crater. A measuring instrument is aligned with them and the direct calculation is made. The "Side Spray" method involves placing a stake in the centre of the crater and two more at the end of the lines of side spray, that is the pattern of damage to either side of the crater. These have to be equidistant from the centre stake. Using a length of wire, two arcs are struck forward of the fuse furrow and at the point of intersection a further stake is planted. The direction measuring instrument is aligned to this stake and the centre stake and the direction is ascertained. With regards to mortars, the typical crater has the ground at the front of the crater undercut by the fuse burying itself in a small tunnel. When the mortar shell impacts, it explodes and the tail fin is going further in the same direction due to its kinetic energy. To the back of the crater the ground is scarred by blast and frameworks (what we saw before) into a distinctive pattern of strakes radiating from the point of detonation. It was clear on the exhibits we showed before. Generally, the strakes end on a straight line perpendicular to the line of flight of the shell. So three methods of crater analysis can be used. The "Main Axis" method that I already explained with the previous exhibits; the "Splinter Groove" method that one uses two stakes for that, one along the main axis of the fuse tunnel and another perpendicular to it, laid along the edge of the damaged strakes. The measuring instrument is aligned with the stake from the fuse tunnel forward of the crater and the measurement is taken. The "Fuse Tunnel" method uses a single stake placed in the fuse tunnel, like we saw on one of the first exhibits I showed on mortar impact, and the measuring instrument is aligned with it, froward of the crater. All these methods enable a compass bearing and direction in degrees, like I showed also on the exercise we did, and the direction in degrees or "mils", like it is often used in the military, are determined to a high degree of accuracy. Then examination of all the fragments that are found on site help to determine which shell and which weapon was used for the shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: This all means that you have a clear picture of the directions and where from they come, how far away they were fired, etc.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like I said before, the difficulty is with the range of course because it is important to have witnesses, the sun is important, gun flash, whatever. Crater analysis is very good to have the direction and it is very accurate for direction.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you combine these different methods, questions with witnesses and doing these analyses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. We did a full investigation, that means we do not only rely on technical evidence but we always do like a complete police investigation. So we interviewed witnesses, victims and every possible item we could use to discover the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you have also a set of examples from different times of this siege from mid '92 up to '95?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Would you please go through it and show us what happened in these certain instances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For certain of these files I will go back to some of the exhibits we saw before and go a little more bit into time maybe.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the first shelling we investigated was the shelling that happened on 27th May 1992. I want to show for that Exhibit 93, please. So mortar shell hit a crowded street where a lot of people were in a bread line like I told before. I think it was in Vase Miskina Street, one of the pedestrians streets.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Light again, please, to make it easier to see the pictures. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So this was in Vase Miskina Street, a pedestrian street in the centre of Sarajevo. In this shelling 17 civilians were killed and 111 were injured. The direction of fire was from a hillside position on Trebevic mountain which was VSA or VRS controlled. The confrontation lines were about one kilometre away from this impact. Can I have the next one please. So like I said before, you see that nobody was safe in this indiscriminate shelling. You see the photo of a young child who was killed in this specific shelling. The next one please. A woman who was killed in the same, very same shelling. Like you see, we only show a couple of victims. Like I said, in this shelling there were 17 people killed and 111 injured. Another shelling we investigated happened on 3rd July '92 where several rounds were fire by a Bosnian Serb tank at a group of people in and around a cherry in Grbavica. That is in the north Sarajevo. The tank crew had a clear view to the target. Both Grbavica and the place where the tank was placed were on an elevated position. Seven of the people, including children under three, were killed in this incident and three others were injured. Another shelling happened on 1st June 1993 and that was during the Muslim holiday of Bajram. A football tournament was held and organised in Dobrinja, a residential settlement. There were some 200 spectators present and about two hours after the start two 82 millimetre shells fell on the location. Twelve people were killed here and over 100 injured. You will remember the photos I showed you earlier in my testimony about the crater analysis, the exercise we did. Crater we examined is one of the two craters created by this shelling. People were playing soccer there on the parking lot. On 26th June '93, 120 millimetre artillery shell hit a group of young people in alley between Hendina 6 and Dragice Pravice 5 in the Bistrik area of Sarajevo. Can we maybe go back to Exhibit 74? So that is south of the city here. Seven people were killed and 28 were injured, all under 21. There were reports of shelling the next days during the funerals of the people that were killed. On 12th July '93 a shell was fired on a line of civilians waiting for water at a distribution tap in Dobrinja. Twelve people were killed there and 16 injured. We can maybe go back to Exhibit 119, please. So that is the photo you saw before with all the cannisters. So people were on the left side of the road queuing for a water pump that was just behind this house on the left side. Exhibit 120, please. So here at the right-hand side, right of the man standing there, was the entrance to the yard where the pump was. People were queuing here in the street and you see a couple of bodies covered by plastic. The next one please. I explained this exhibit before. The next shelling I want to talk about happened on 28th November'93 when a 120 millimetre shell hit a group of people in Dobrovoljacka Street killing five, injuring six. On 6th December '93, a 122 artillery shell was fired at the Ciglane area hitting an overpass above Djure Dakovica Street and exploding on civilians gathered in a small open air market, an area which was frequently shelled. Six people were killed there and 14 injured. On 22nd January '94 -- can I have Exhibit 96? -- around 1 o'clock in the afternoon three mortar shells were fired on open ground where a group of children between five and 12 years of age were sledding in the snow. This was in Alipasino Polje. It is a residential area; you see all the apartments around. Six of these children were killed and five were wounded. On 4th February '94, three 120 millimetre mortar shells landed in Dobrinja residential area killing nine civilians, injuring three. These people were waiting at distribution points for humanitarian aid. If I can have Exhibit 99 for this, please. So you will see the place where all the people were waiting for humanitarian aid. The next one, please. I will show you another time the victims of the shelling. Like I said, nine were killed and 23 were injured. The next one, please. The next one. OK, that is enough for this shelling. I do not want to show them all again. I have shown them. The day after on 5th February '94, a 120 millimetre shell hit Markale market in the old town of Sarajevo, the market was crowded with shoppers and 67 civilians were killed and over 200 people were injured. The shell was heard being fired from behind Spicasta Stijena, which is Bosnian Serb held territory, and then exploded down town where there were no military targets, as with the other areas of course referred to in our case investigations. On 30th October 1994, a 120 millimetre shell was fired from Vojkovici -- I can have maybe Exhibit 74 again, that is about here in this area -- fired to two civilians Igman Road in Hrasnica. There was some kind of stop there and people tried to earn some money to get luggage for people. One person was killed here, one civilian, and 15 others were wounded. On 8th November 84 an 82 millimetre mortar shell landed at half past 3 in the afternoon, and two more shells landed at about half past 5 in Livanjska Street in Sarajevo. One civilian was killed, seven injured. On 17th November 1994 a 120 millimetre shell exploded in Ulice Partizanska in Hrasnica that you see in the south of Sarajevo here. This was very heavily shelled through the whole siege. That shell killed two children, injuring two adult females and injured another child. On 12th December 1994 an 82 millimetre shell exploded in the yard of a civilian dwelling at Donji Kartal Street No. 6 which is about here in Sarajevo. One elderly man of about 70 years old was chopping wood, was killed and his wife was injured. On 22nd December '94 two 76 millimetre artillery shells hit a flea market in the old town, in the old town of Sarajevo here in the east, from the direction of Bosnian Serb positions from Trebevic mountain. Two people were killed and seven injured. On 12th March '95, a 120 millimetre shell landed on the yard of the Muslim secondary school, which is about here in the old town of Sarajevo, killing one civilian, this building is clearly in an area exclusively comprised of shops, businesses and cultural buildings and well inside the confrontation line as can you see. On 7th April 1995, if we can go back to Exhibit 136 for that, a modified air bomb was fired from the Bosnian-Serb held Ilidza at 9 o'clock in the morning. The weapon impacted in Hrasnica causing extensive damage to a number of civilian dwellings like we see on Exhibit 137. So killing one civilian, Exhibit 138, and injuring three others. Can I have Exhibit 74, again, please? So the air bomb landed here in Hrasnica fired from Ilidza here in the west. On 12th April 1995 at 11.55 a 60 millimetre shell exploded near the railway station which is about here, near the railway station in Sarajevo which was not operating since the start of hostilities. Seven civilians were wounded in this attack. On 18th June 1995 at 11.40 a 120 millimetre mortar shell hit a group of civilians in a water line. We can go back to Exhibit 110 for that. So that is what I told you before about the Simon Bolava Elementary School where a water pump was placed here. The next one, please. To recapitulate, the shell hit the wall here, exploded, stabilized and fell here and you see here the stabilizer. In this shelling seven people were killed and 12 were wounded out of a group of 50 other people. Can I have the next one, please? The next one, please. So you see another time an elderly man is the victim. The next one, please. The next one, please. The next one please. I show you these pictures again to make clear that the shelling was really indiscriminate and everybody was affected by that. On 28th June '95 a modified air bomb was fired at around 9.20 and struck the TV building and it had been launched again from Ilidza from the west of Sarajevo. One person was killed and 28 injured. You can maybe show again Exhibit 74. So, it was fired from this area -- I am not all always that handy with these things -- fired from this area and fired to there. On 19th July 1995 a 120 millimetre shell hit close to a private house in Sarajevo and shrapnel killed a 12 year old boy in the bathroom of his house. On 22nd August '95 an observation post was shelled at 10 o'clock. The observation post was located in Emerovica north east of Sarajevo. Six Egyptian UN shoulders got injured, two of them very severe. The first shelled landed just outside of the observation post and the following four landed in the observation post, which indicated a deliberate adjusting of fire. The second shell caused injuries while the soldiers were running from the house to the shelter. On 28th August 1995 between 11 and 10 past 11 five 120 millimetre mortar shells landed in the old town of Sarajevo. We can go back to Exhibit 87 for that. So one of these shells exploded in the Mula-Mustafe Baseskije Street, so by the entrance of the City Market in the centre of the old town. The market and the streets were crowded with people that day. So the result of this shelling was that 43 people got killed and 75 injured. One of the four other shells that landed in the neighbourhood injured eight more people. Can I have the next exhibit please? So again you can clearly see the pattern of the crater of this mortar shell and all the blood around the place of impact. You can imagine when we go back to the previous exhibit, Exhibit 87, like I told before, the 120 millimetre shell has a legal radius of 54 metres and a danger area of 500 metres, you can imagine what happens when a shell explodes in a crowded street and a lot of people are walking into this street. Can I have Exhibit 89, please? The next one, please. So you can see the amount of blood around the place of impact, the rest of the UN bodies because at this moment the victims were already taken away to the morgue and or hospital. The next one please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecuting counsel, we have already seen these documents I believe?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think that what the witness wanted to show us were the techniques that were used for seeing where these projectiles came from, etc. So, if it is possible and if it in no way impedes demonstration, you would like to carry on, maybe we could just pursue. We have already seen these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We just went through the examples and these were shown again to put them in the context of where things happened. (To the witness): I have some conclusive questions to your presentation about the shelling and sniping of Sarajevo. I note in your description from this example that you say it was a 76 millimetre, that it was an 82 millimetre, it was 120 millimetre mortar, etc. Are there any technical problems to determine exactly what kind of ammunition was used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Most of the time you find or detailing the stabilizing of the mortar shell, you find fragments of the shells and from these fragments you can determine which shell was used by the ----

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: There is no technical problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we have people who are specialised in these matters. People who are specialised can easily determine which shell and which weapon had fired these shells.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just state before we leave this subject, when was the first day of shelling and when was the last day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first day was in May '92 and it ended with the Dayton Agreement in November/December '95.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, I have just one subject left, and that is the investigation of the shelling of civilians in Tuzla on one day, 25th May 1995. (To the witness): Could you briefly tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. On 25th May 1995 all the safe areas in Bosnia were shelled by the Bosnian Serb army, probably as a sort of revenge for NATO air strikes. The explosion I investigated was an explosion of a 130 millimetre gun shell and the shell landed that evening shortly before 9 o'clock on a square in Kapija area in the centre of Tuzla. It was the day of the youth and a lot of young people were gathered on the square and on terraces. In this shelling 72 civilians got killed and over 100 got injured.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was this the only shelling of that city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There has been more shelling of Tuzla. Yes. We maybe can bring in another exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, we can conclude the questioning by showing some clips of a video. Can you dim the lights, please. (The video clip was shown).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside a hospital. You can see again these water canisters, people were getting water. This is another site where children were sledding. Victims. You will see again what kind of a view they had from the hills towards Sarajevo. You will see the view you have to the city. There is the sniper alley on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes my examination and I thank you Mr. Van Hecke.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. It is 10 minutes past one. So we need not pursue, Mr. Heck, just the questions. Do you have a question, Judge Odio Benito?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Van Hecke, would you say that the Bosnian Serb Army was the organisation responsible the shelling and sniping campaign against the people of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The weapons used in this shelling and sniping campaign are normally used only by the regular army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, these weapons are used in regular warfare normally, so against enemy troops, but in this case they were clearly used against civilians within the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But these kinds of weapons could be also by a paramilitary organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everyone who has kind these kinds of weapons can use them of course. So it is, let us say, except for the improvised air bomb, these are normal weapons to be used by an army.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where historical or religious monument severely damaged or destroyed in Sarajevo during the siege of the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were several cultural buildings which were destroyed, like the National Library, for instance, in Sarajevo, mosques, churches, those kinds of buildings, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Finally, in your opinion how did the people survive this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, with difficulty, but I think people are used to improvise, so a lot of people lived almost all through the siege in their basements, in cellars and tried to protect themselves from the shelling and or sniping, but like I said before, they had to come out now and again to have basic things like water, food and whatever. So they had to try to find shelter in their basements and every strong place they could find.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Because, as far as I understood, they were completely isolated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were completely isolated from the rest of the world.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The rest of the world?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Van Hecke, in this very thorough investigation which you undertook, did you come across any indication that some of the sites which were shelled like the secondary school, the hospital, they concealed weapons or ammunition or was there a place from which any resistance could come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is a point of our investigation. We investigated very thoroughly that there were no moves by Bosnian government troops, or there was no military target even in the neighbourhood of the places that were targeted by these shellings.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: There was no firing back from anywhere in Sarajevo during these shellings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There has been firing from the confrontation lines, but most of the sites we investigated are far away from these confrontation lines and you can miss a target in that distance.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The last picture you gave us of Dr. Karadzic, were they on what you called the snipers' line? Where were they from? Was he watching the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you see it was taken from the south of the city, and you saw the yellowish building down there, that was the Holiday Inn Hotel and it was laying on what they called sniper alley. So the main road going from the east, from the old city to the west where the new suburbs of Sarajevo were. That is what they called sniper alley.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, and the snipers were around in that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: They were still around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We have done investigations of sniping coming from that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just one question on the sources of these pictures, not the video, the pictures. Is it the Sarajevo police investigations? What is the source of those photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, most of the photos are of a source of Bosnian police investigations. Some are taken by myself or my colleagues when we were in Sarajevo. Like we had, for instance, Exhibits 76 to 78 where I showed the barricades that were photos taken by ourselves when we were in Sarajevo to do the investigations. Most of the photos of the shelling files were, of course, photos taken by the Bosnian police investigators. If that answers your question, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Finally, prosecuting counsel, you have done with Mr. Van Hecke. The Tribunal would like to thank you for your testimony. Now it is quarter past one. We shall resume at quarter to three this afternoon. (1.15 p.m.) (Luncheon Adjournment) (2.45 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution, would you please introduce the following witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. The Prosecution would call Tarik Kupusovic to the stand, please. MR. TARIK KUPUSOVIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good day to you. Can you hear me, first of all? THE WITNESS (In translation): Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you hear me? There is a solemn declaration you will have to read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, sir. You, I take it, will be introducing yourself. Before giving the floor to the counsel for the Prosecution, I would like to tell you that you have been called by the Prosecution in the cases relating to Messrs. Mladic and Karadzic. The Tribunal would like to thank you, of course, for coming here at the Prosecution's request. We would also like to tell you that you are here before an international body, before the International Criminal Tribunal, and that you should speak without any fear of any kind and as freely as possible. Counsel for the Prosecution, you have the floor to introduce your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, would you please state your full name and spell it for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Tarik Kupusovic, T-A-R-I-K K-U-P-U-S-O-V-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Sir, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Is your family from the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My family has been living in Sarajevo for over 400 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What did you do before the fighting broke out in Sarajevo in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a civil engineer and I have a PhD in engineering. I worked as Professor at the Civil Engineering Faculty and Director of the Hydraulics Research Institute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution, there does not seem to be any sound in the visitors' gallery. This is a public hearing. We have not taken any special measures. None have been requested on your part or on the part of the witness, so this a public hearing. So I would ask that we stop for the time being; that we see with the technicians exactly what is up. I do apologise, sir. Then we will have ask you to repeat once we get this straightened out. Thank you. There is no transcript on the screens either.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are going to have to repeat, Prosecuting counsel, so if you would start from the beginning. I can see the visitors' gallery and I will right away if the sound is not coming through. Please be so kind, sir, as to start from the beginning again. You have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Mr. Kupusovic, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Apparently, it is still not working, I am afraid. I am afraid we are going to have to adjourn for a few minutes because it would be appropriate for the people in the visitors' gallery to follow these proceedings so the meeting is adjourned. (Adjourned for a short time)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Registrar, you said it was working but not perfectly, so perhaps you could explain in particular for the visitors' gallery to make sure everyone hears you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. In the public gallery the loud speakers do not work in the public gallery, but the earphones do work so if everyone in the public gallery could put on his earphones, then they can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You have the floor, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, would you please tell the court where you were born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Is your family from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my family has been in Sarajevo for over 400 years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What did you do before the fighting began in 1992 in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a civil engineer, I have a PhD in Technical Sciences and I worked as Professor at the Engineering Faculty in Sarajevo and I was also a Director of the Hydraulics Research Institute in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Where were you living when the fighting began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was living in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Where is to be Dobrinja located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dobrinja is a new part of the city near the airport, built as an Olympic village, as the village for the media people, for the Winter Olympics in 1984 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would you please describe for the court the various municipalities that comprise Sarajevo before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sarajevo had four urban areas, municipalities, and also six surrounding municipalities, Pale, Vogasa, Hadzici, Trnivo, Ilijas and Hadzici. The urban municipalities were the old town, the centre the new Sarajevo and the new town. That makes up a total of 2,500 square metres; the urban part being about 13 kilometres by four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the war, were you involved in any sort of politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took part in the elections in 1990. I ran for the office on behalf of the Democratic Action Party in the election area of the old town where I was born. I was elected a councillor in the Assembly, in the city Assembly, and I was the chief of the caucus of my party until I was elected Mayor of the City.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Before you were elected Mayor what were your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a City Council. We had regular meetings once a month. There were also several meetings and arrangements between the Presidents of the caucuses in the parliament, so I had a lot of amateur activities. I did not work professional in politics, but only as a delegate, as a representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Before the war started, how many political parties were there in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were eight parties. Eight parties were voted into the City Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Before the war started did these political parties co-operate together in working in the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, naturally, they did both as parties and also as representatives. Members of the City Assembly and the Presidents of the caucuses made arrangements all the time and communicated with each other in preparing the sessions of the City Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we would like to introduce Exhibit 176. It is a recently obtained exhibit so it is not in your binders. We have copies. It is a newspaper statement and we have translations on the back of the actual statement itself. If we could distribute those to the court, please? We would like to show the article itself in its Cyrillic version on the overhead projector. (To the witness) Sir, do you recognise Exhibit 176?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would you tell the court what it is, please, and then read it into the record and our translators will translate it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a declaration from the meeting of representatives of all parliamentary parties and Presidents of the caucuses in the City Assembly, issued on 19th April 1992 when shooting had already started in Sarajevo, but we still hoped for a democratic environment in which the situation would resolve itself favourably. "At this meeting", I am reading, "At a session of the Sarajevo City Assembly held on 19th April 1992, attended by representatives of all parliamentary parties whose delegates constitute the city Assembly, chaired by the City Assembly Chairman, Muhamed Kresevljakovic, a joint statement was adopted and signed. "No-one from the City, the Republic or Europe has the right to negotiate the division of Sarajevo on behalf of the citizens of Sarajevo. The City of Sarajevo with a history of more than 500 years of coexistence in a multi-cultural, multi-confessional and multi-national community is indivisible. "A concept of modern European civilian life is being defended in Sarajevo; Sarajevo is the capital of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina where all human rights and freedoms are respected, and because of that we say that no-one has the right to endanger the lives, peace and property of the citizens and the cultural and historical heritage and natural resources of Sarajevo". This was signed by Miodrag Jankovic on behalf of the Reform Party of Sarajevo; Bozidar Popara on behalf of the Serbian Democratic Party as the President of the Party's caucus for the City of Sarajevo; Tarik Kupusovic, that is myself, on behalf of the party of Democratic Action; Anto Zelic on behalf of the Croatian Democratic Party; Slobodan Primorac on behalf of the Party of Democratic Changes; Esad Afgan on behalf of the Muslim Bosniak organisation; Nijaz Nurkovic on behalf of the Liberals; Spahic on behalf of the Democratic Socialist Alliance and Muhamed Kresevljakovic, the then Mayor of Sarajevo. Let me just explain briefly, this text was published in Cyrillic because Oslobodjenje, the main paper of Sarajevo, long before the war and also long time into the war when the technical facilities made it possible, was published so that one page was published in the Latin alphabet and the other one in the Cyrillic alphabet, and individual articles on one page were sometimes published in Cyrillic and sometimes in Latin in order to emphasis the equality of the two alphabets in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: The date of this session mentioned in this statement was 19th April 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: The leader of the SDS in Sarajevo was one of the signatories to this particular statement, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he signed it himself. But when this was published in the papers, Radovan Karadzic relieved him from that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When was he relieved from his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately when this statement was made public. Obviously, he had not asked for permission for Karadzic, so when he signed it, it did not fit the policies pursued by the leader of the Bosnian Serbian Party, Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. After the war began in Sarajevo, did you serve in any public office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This meeting was the result of the fact because all the 120 elected representatives could not gather; only representatives of individual parties were able to come to this meeting. So the total number of those who attended the meeting was only 80. By the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and by laws that had been adopted from the previous, from the former Yugoslavia, it was stipulated that in case that the City Assembly could not meet, that the presidency should be formed, the Assembly's presidency, so that it is made up of representatives of the parties which participate in the City Assembly, Mayor, the deputy Mayor, the Chief of the Civil Protection and the Police. In this way, the presidency was formed, was set up, of which I was a member until I was elected Mayor of the City. It really took over all the competences of the Assembly and was the highest civil authority in the City of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were there Serbs and Croatians also serving on the wartime Sarajevo presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, naturally, there were two Croats, the President of the Croatian Democratic Party and the Vice Mayor, and there were three or four Serbs depending on the time because they took turns among themselves of a total of 11 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When you became the Mayor did you have Serbs working in the office with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. The chief of my protocol was a Serb because he had done the same office and he continued as a professional. There were four or five Serbs of a total of about 20 people who made up the core of the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When were you actually elected as Mayor of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the first ultimatum by NATO in February 1994, there was a peaceful period in Sarajevo and the City Assembly met, had a session. The Mayor before that time, who served before that time, had been appointed on a diplomatic position. In March again new candidates were put up and I was elected as Mayor of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How long did you end up serving as Mayor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost two years, until March 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: As Mayor, what municipalities came within your control and could you compare that with what your authority would have been before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officially, I kept control over all the 10 municipalities but, in reality, it was reduced to parts of the four of the core, City core, and a part of the fifth municipality, only a small portion of that municipality, Vogasa. The duties of the Mayor normally in peaceful time and in wartime, I continued to do that in wartime, to represent the City, to prepare and chair the sessions of the City Assembly, and also to take care of the international affairs of the City, international relations. The preparation of the City Assembly sessions means co-ordinating of the work directly -- of the people directly responsible for the functioning of the City infrastructure. A large part of my time and effort was devoted to finding alternative solutions to what in all other cities in the world is a routine matter: providing bread, water, power and other basic necessities necessary to the functioning of a City.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Sir, would you please just take a few moments and describe for the court what it was like to live in Sarajevo before the fighting began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the beginning of the conflict, before the beginning of the siege of Sarajevo, Sarajevo was a modern, European City with a contemporary infrastructure. The first town which obtained international loan for the improving infrastructure, about 30 years ago, was Sarajevo when the President of the World Bank was the well-known McNamara. Later on, in the 80s, as part of the preparations for the Olympic games, Sarajevo acquired a very modern system of power supply, water supply was improved, the purification of water was improved, the City transportation and all the other functions of the City were exactly equal to those of any other European City. The inhabitants of Sarajevo were particularly proud of this, because the modern water supply systems and the City transit system and the electric power in Sarajevo were used towards the end of the last century because Sarajevo was an experiment to Austria/Hungary by which Bosnia and Herzegovina and Sarajevo were ruled for over 40 years before World War I. The democratic processes in Yugoslavia in 1991, at least they looked like democratic processes, reprivatisation of firms and companies and businesses started, and many firms had very high profits and wages and people were very happy indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did the citizens of Sarajevo and, indeed, the citizens of the former Yugoslavia have any special feelings towards the City of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sarajevo is the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the central Republic of the former Yugoslavia, centrally located, where for over 400 years both the Bosnian Muslims and Serbs and Croats and Jews lived together, and members of all other nationalities and ethnic groups in harmony and simply happy. It is frequently said that the only place in the world where within an area of 400 metres there is a large cathedral, a Jewish synagogue, an orthodox church and a mosque, where in a sound harmony you can hear the calls to prayer for all these places of worship. Especially the Olympic games lent a modern spirit to the City of Sarajevo, and a feeling of membership in Europe and in the world community, and especially it had a secure place in the future of Europe and the world at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: If we could please have the lights dimmed and we would like to have Exhibit 149 brought up on the screen. It is 3080. Sir, would you tell the court, please, what this view represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a view of Sarajevo from Trebevic, Mount Trebevic. It is a small mountain near Sarajevo. It is a favourite resort place for Sarajevans which was accessible by cable car or by road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What was Trebevic like before the fighting began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has a lot of pastures and meadows and woods and many paths, pedestrian paths, benches, picnic areas, to enjoy the view of Sarajevo and several small cafes and restaurants for resting and for recreation and not only for Sarajevans but also the visitors of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Was there a cable car that serviced the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you can see a pillar of the cable car from the City. It took you 12 minutes to go from the down town Sarajevo to Vidikovac which offered the best view of Sarajevo, the old part and the central part of Sarajevo, and the new part closer to the airport cannot be seen in this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What happened to Trebevic once the fighting began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of a sudden, we discovered that Trebevic was filled with cannon and artillery pieces, tanks and other weapons which were shooting at the City; not only Trebevic, but other surrounding hills around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, for point of reference, we would just point out that the video tape that was seen this morning with the accused Karadzic showing a Russian poet how the troops were sniping from the hills is in the Trebevic area, for a point of reference. Sir, did the JNA before the fighting actually began take any actions that eventually led to them participating in the fighting itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. All the artillery pieces were placed, in fact, by the JNA around Sarajevo, and explained it by saying to those who were interested that this is part of the routine manoeuvres by the army, conducted by the army, especially on Trebevic. In other places, it was in far away villages so it was not seen by citizens of Sarajevo. But, immediately before the hostilities, in March 1992, Trebevic was made off bounds to civilians because of the alleged manoeuvres by the former Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Before the fighting began did the JNA take any actions with regard to the Sarajevo airport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As early as March 1992, the former JNA occupied Sarajevo airport and it stopped being a civilian airport and became a military one. Except for the presence of the weapons the, tanks and the troops, there were only military planes used at the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you notice any activity with regard to the families of the soldiers and officers of the JNA before the fighting began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was living in Dobrinja, as I said. I could see from my window, I could see the airport, and I also went to work by car and I passed by the airport. I saw many people who were going to the airport, some of them on foot, others by military buses. Obviously (and this was later confirmed) they were families of the officers of the JNA originally from Serbia who were being evacuated from Sarajevo. Many of the officers of the JNA who had been Bosnian Serbs had already evacuated their families, had also evacuated their families, to Belgrade and further on. At the time, this is before the real beginning of the war, there was an euphoria among those inhabitants as to who will leave the City in a more comfortable manner until the situation calms down again. However, in relation to the other -- in relation to the size of the population, it was a very small number of people who left the City at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: If you could take a few moments and think back to the days just before the fighting began and the war broke out. What was happening in the City of Sarajevo and what were the people's attitudes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We all believed that after the Peace Treaty was signed for Croatia on 1st January 1992 by Presidents Tudjman, Milosevic and the international community, a similar war would be avoided in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In Sarajevo itself, there were movements in favour of peace, organisations which spread the conviction that there was no reason for war in Bosnia, and that all misunderstandings may and must be resolved peacefully by political means. There was an excitement in the town because of the departure of the members of the families of the JNA officers from Serbia, but this was expressed more as a regret that they do not believe in peace, and that they are victims of a propaganda that causes them to leave the City in which they had been living for over 20 or 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Had anyone enquired with any of the SDS leaders about the artillery that had been placed in the hills surrounding Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that the President of the municipality of Stari Grad and the then town Mayor also enquired about this, and they received answers that these were exercises and that the Yugoslav People's Army was neutral, that it was protecting the peace and that it would protect Sarajevo from any kind of war or conflict. Whether they believed this or not, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: At some point were barricades erected in the City?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first barricades in the City appeared on March 2nd after the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were put up by the activists of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What did leaders in the SDS party say about the erection of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said it was in protest on the part of their party against the referendum as such, and they wished to demonstrate their non-recognition of the results of the referendum which gave more than a two-thirds majority in favour of an independent and sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina on the basis of which it was recognised after a few days by the European Community and the United Nations. Already at the time there was sporadic shooting when the first barricades were erected, but a large crowd of civilians, children and inhabitants of Sarajevo, carried slogans "We do not want barricades, we do not want war, we want peace". They forced the barricades to come down that very afternoon. Then, for Sarajevo, they were seen only as an unsuccessful demonstration of power on behalf of the Serbian Democratic Party. Then it was only later that we learnt what firing and grenades really meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When and how did the fighting actually start in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout March talks were conducted among party leaders and the Yugoslav People's Army, and the situation was tense but the City was still leading a normal life, one might say. On April 5th or 6th, in the night between 5th and the 6th, barricades emerged again and again a large movement for peace in Sarajevo and many other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina people had come by buses to demonstrate their wish for the preservation of peace, for the preservation of life together and the preservation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a homeland of all its citizens and peoples. Then there was fire from the seat of the Serbian Democratic Party which was situated in The Holiday Inn, and that was the beginning of sniping and shelling of the City itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When the fighting actually started, did the people of Sarajevo think that it would last very long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we all thought that this would be resolved even tomorrow. We thought a meeting or two, and even the worst forecasts expected two months, it to take two months, for as long as Dubrovnik was exposed to attacks and a siege on the part of those who did it. That was the feeling of all of us, in April, in May and several months. We did not expect it to go on more than the autumn. Perhaps that was an indication of our naiveness because it was inconceivable how anyone could attack a City, the citizens, in which there were absolutely no military targets, and we considered this to be madness and that only lunatics could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Had the City made any preparations for war or for any type of siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No ---

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the atmosphere was not such that people believed in a siege or attack against the town, and that was one thing. Secondly, the preparations officially within the military and the civilian structures working for the army envisaged simply the possibility of an external attack and those plans were quite useless for the situation in the City.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You speak of the uselessness of the Civil Defence plans; in fact, in the case of an outside attack, it is somewhat ironic, I think, where was the City Hall to relocate from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly in the event of war was to relocate to Pale where it would continue to function. Actually, Karadzic moved to Pale and it became quite irrelevant. An alternative to Pale or the first mobile spot for the town Mayor and the authorities of the City was Debolo Brdo, a locality very close to the City Hall on the slopes of Trebevic, which was actually under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army at the time and to which also there was no access and, therefore, the Town Hall and all the bodies remained in the City where they had operated in peace time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: After the fighting started, were there many Sarajevo Serbs who decided not to join the accused Radovan Karadzic and his party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the very beginning and throughout the duration of the siege, there was 40 to 50,000 Sarajevan Serbs living in Sarajevo who decided not to join Karadzic. Among those 80,000 that left the City, Serbs who left the City, it is estimated that about half joined Karadzic and the other half were refugees who were scattered all over the world. Therefore, out of the total of 120,000 Serbs that used to live in Sarajevo before the war, about one-third joined Karadzic, one-third stayed in the City and a third left the City together with a large number of Bosniaks and Croats and others who simply could not stand all the troubles of a four-year siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What type of propaganda did the Serbian radio and TV stations broadcast regarding the Sarajevan Serbs who stayed loyal to the multi-ethnic City?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They called them and they are calling them traitors of Serbs, or servants of the Muslim regime, and various other such epithets which placed them in an even worse position than the other inhabitants of Sarajevo who are not Serbs. Of course, there were many mixed marriages in Sarajevo. 30 per cent were mixed marriages before the war. The children of mixed marriages considered themselves rather Yugoslav, most frequently they considered themselves Bosnian without affiliating themselves with any of the ethnic groups. For Karadzic's propaganda, if one of the parents were Serbs, then those children were also traitors because they had the courage to marry somebody of a different faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move now to another topic, that of the shelling of Sarajevo: would you please tell the court when the shelling of the City actually began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shelling of Sarajevo began in April, but then it was a few incidents, as we thought at the time. It was not on a daily or regular basis, but only on a number of occasions Stari Grad was exposed to shelling, a couple of places in the new part of the City, and this was at the time considered to be incidents provoked by extremists, both by the Yugoslav People's Army which still was, apparently, neutral and by the United Nations forces who were in the City.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: In April did the Serb forces damage one of the trolley or tram depots in the City?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one night a tram depot, or the garage of the depot, was shelled and the next morning the trams could not work and municipal transport came to a standstill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What did Sarajevo's Director of Transportation do after that incident in April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Director of the Urban Transportation was a friend of Momcilo Krajisnik's before the war. The phones were still operating and he called him up and asked, "Why did you do this? Why were you destroying the tram?" Krajisnik's answer was that this was an act by a lunatic and that he would take care that it was not repeated. When Krajisnik said this, the trams started operating again in the afternoon and for sometime they continued operating until May 2nd. This was mid April we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Where were you when the heavy shelling began on May 2nd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Together with my wife and children, I happened to be visiting my wife's parents in Marindvor which is in the very centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What did you do when the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With my family, I was just getting ready to go home to Dobrinja, and when the tram was set on fire at Skenderija and the shelling actually started, I returned immediately to the apartment of my in-laws. We spent the first two-and-a-half months of the war there because there was no City transportation and Dobrinja on that day was on a twofold blockade. Sarajevo as a whole was blocked and Dobrinja was blocked as well within that general blockade. The next day the telephones were still working. In the afternoon the post office burnt down, but we learnt that the City in which we had lived that half the flats had been destroyed and set on fire by an attack from the airport which was held by the Yugoslav People's Army and with several transporters from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What happened to your home and property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything was plundered and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How did the people of Sarajevo initially respond to this first shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a terrible shock. People just could not understand what was happening. It was inconceivable. It appeared to have no justification. Simply, we could not believe that the war had begun. Most of our time was spent in the basements or in other premises which appeared to be safer. All communication ceased because the City transport stopped. The telephones were not working. We could not walk in the streets because in the sporadic lulls in between the shelling people were simply under shock and they feared what was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What were some of the first targets of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the railway stations -- everything was a target. It was difficult to say what was a target. Occasionally, Stari Grad or the old City was shelled, then the centre, then some new parts of the City, some individual buildings, but not a single part of the City was spared a shell or two or some other fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Do you think that any of the selected early targets had symbolic value to the City and the citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, when the national library burnt down it was a great shock. When the hall, both the indoor and outside venue of the Olympic games and the stadium in Kosovo were hit, these had symbolic and actual value. Then again business premises, the premises of the government and the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were among the first targets of shelling. When the Oriental Studies Institute and, in addition to the National Library, several monuments of historic value of Sarajevo burnt down, that was when the word "urbicide" was developed, that is, the killing of monuments, a derivation of the word "genocide".

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did General Mladic ever make a statement regarding why he thought it was necessary to shell the Olympic stadium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when Zetra was shelled, he first said that the Sarajevo authorities were holding captured Serbs there. When the response was, "Surely, then they would not shell Serbs", then the response was that it was an ammunition depot. However, it is a sports hall in which there were four or five sports rifles in a shop selling hunting weapons. This was in the window of the shop. It was not being used and it would not be used anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time if we could have the lights dimmed again? We have some additional photos. First, if we could have Exhibit 150, No. 3070, brought up on the screen? You also have copies in your binders of these photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is in this morning's case file, is it, the one we received this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The actual coloured photographs are in the binders by exhibit number. Then we will also be showing them on the computer screen.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What number was that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 150, 150.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. BOWERS (To the witness): Sir, would you please take a look at Exhibit 50 and tell the court what this photograph is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The photograph is of the Magribija mosque which, during the Ottoman rule, was on the edge of the City and, with the spread of the City, it was in the centre and it was of unique architectural and artistic beauty. You can see the minaret destroyed and the whole roof virtually destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you see this mosque shortly after it was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the time, in May 1992, I was living with my in-laws and this happened in the night of May 17th, between 17th and 18th May, when from a mortar launcher, a multiple mortar launcher which destroys targets of a larger area, the whole City was shelled, from the old part of the City to the new. We spent all that night until 4 a.m. in the cellars. When the shelling stopped, after a short nap in the morning, I went to get bread with my son. Near the mosque was a place where they were distributing bread. On the way, we were looking at the effects of the shelling. One of the worse shocks I got was when I saw the mosque exactly as it is depicted on this photograph, one of the most beautiful architectural and historical buildings in Sarajevo which, thanks to good men, has already been partly reconstructed, except for the minaret which requires a longer period of time for reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What were your personal thoughts when you happened upon this destruction of this mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me, this was like the end of the world, the end of Sarajevo, but only of course for a few hours, because after all the City is composed of people and the people will rebuild it when this madness of destroying such buildings comes to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could have Exhibit 151 brought up on the screen, that is, 3071, Exhibit 151? Sir, what does this photograph depict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is also a mosque, but completely destroyed. It is of a more recent date, maybe 10 or 30 years old. It was built in the old part of the City, and it was obviously a target by the barbarians who were destroying what makes a city a city.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit 152, that number is 3072? Sir, what does this photograph depict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a large catholic church at Stupe, a part of the City of Sarajevo, where several thousand Catholics lived. That church was also virtually burnt down and destroyed in May. All that remains were the walls and the remnants that you can tell it used to be a church.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Now if we could have Exhibit 153, please, that is No. 3073? Sir, would you please describe this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the building of the National and University Library of Sarajevo in flames from inflammable shells and rockets which set on fire the documentation of the library, documents speaking of the history of Bosnia, some of them up to 800 years old, up to the more recent ones. Everything has been destroyed. All that remains are some fragments of documents that happened to be elsewhere when this occurred and only the ruins of the building remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit 154, please, 3074? Is this a shot of what remained of the interior of the library?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you can just see the remains of the most beautiful pillars which were a component part of the interior of the library. Let me add, perhaps, that this building served at the beginning of this century as the building of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a separate, autonomous unit within the Austro-Hungarian Empire. It was originally built as the Town Hall, the offices of the town Mayor were there and the formal premises for the festive occasions. 30 years ago, the National and University Libraries were moved into this building when the Town Hall moved to another building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, if we can have the lights brought up now for a while? Sir, as the shelling continued throughout the days and then the months and eventually the years, did it develop into any type of pattern during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It took us some time, the inhabitants of Sarajevo, to grasp some rules in the shelling. Very often, it was peaceful in the morning and then about 11 o'clock several shells would hit. People would scatter from the streets seeking shelter -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt you. The Court Reporter has lost the sound so I think we are going to have to perhaps stop for a few moments -- if the Registry can tell us? So can the Court Reporter hear the proceedings now? No. Let us see now, it is 4 o'clock. I would suggest -- I was hoping to press on for 4.15 but why not have the recess now and then we will pick up at 4.15, 4.20, that is to say, if we can get all these technical matters straightened out. The session is adjourned. (4.00 p.m.) (The court adjourned for a short time)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have the floor, Mr. Bowers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Kupusovic, when we took a break you were describing the patterns or so-called rules that developed with the shelling of the citizens of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after several weeks from the beginning of the shelling we noticed certain regularities which were kept until the end of siege of the city. That meant that early in the morning until 11 o'clock, until about noon, it was quite peaceful. It was rather peaceful. Then between 11.00 and 12.00 three or four shells would explode and people took shelter in basements. Then in the afternoon at irregular intervals when people went out of the basements to bring water or take care of another business, several other, several more shells were fired. During the first two years about 10 people were killed by these shells and several dozens were wounded. The idea was to get the people out of the basements, out of their shelters, after what seemed a relatively peaceful period.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: In your opinion, did the Serbs seem to target civilian gatherings in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very frequently the targets were all civilian gatherings, whether it was at places where they took water or shops, or places where humanitarian aid was distributed, or any other places where people gathered. They could see from the hills quite well and they could target whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What impact did the general shelling and, in particular, the shelling of civilian gatherings have on the citizens of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It had a very demoralizing effect. They tried to make the citizens spend as much time as possible in the shelters and, without mutual communication and pressured by the danger, by risk to their lives, began to lose their feeling of security. Elementary needs such as water, or bread or just meet a friend or visit a friend or a cousin, those possibilities were considerably drastically reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Whenever the Bosnian and Herzegovinian army engaged in any action out on the frontlines, how would the Bosnian-Serb army generally respond to action on the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then Karadzic's Serbs would engage in massive shelling of the city. There was hell let loose in the city itself. Whether it was happening in Bihac or in Gorazde or in the surroundings of the city, the response was invariably massive shelling. This was revenge on civilians, reprisals, especially when the Bosnian Army was successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Sir, just to clarify, not only did the Bosnian Serb army shell the civilian areas of the city when there was action on the frontline around Sarajevo, but they also shelled the city when there were actions outside of Sarajevo in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: At this point we would like to move to the next topic which would be the sniping in the city. Sir, when did the sniping begin in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some sniping on 1st and 2nd March during the first barricades. There were no casualties at the time, but the real sniping began on 6th April. The first victim fell, and that was a student of medicine, Suada Deliberovic, a lady from Dubrovnik, who was doing her studies in Sarajevo. She died. She was killed on the bridge between Marin Dvor and Grbavica in a peace procession which was heading towards the school of the Ministry of the Interior where Karadzic's Serbs were concentrated and the activists of the Serbian Democratic Party. That group wanted to prevent the attack of the city in a peaceful way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did the sniping continue throughout the entire siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was not a single day without several sniper hits, shots, and every day there were several wounded and many parts of the city were exposed to sniping all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did the citizens of Sarajevo come to notice any patterns with the sniping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
