utterances.text: There were no patterns as far as the time of sniping, but in many parts sniping was continual. There were special places that were particularly dangerous. All the localities opened to Trebevic, exposed to Trebevic, or other locations from which sniping occurred. The citizens of Sarajevo, in fact, were lucky when they had fog on the hills around Sarajevo. Then the snipers were fogged in and it was peaceful in Sarajevo. Before the war, the fog in Sarajevo meant unclean air. It was not a sign of good weather, but in wartime it became a sign of security and safety when it was covered with fog.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: In your opinion, what was the intended purpose of the sniping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, it was to kill people, but we can also say that sniping and shelling could have been used to kill many more Sarajevans than they did. The purpose was to keep the city hostage in a way and hopeless in a situation where everything would be controlled by Karadzic's Serbs and that they be lords of peace and war, war and peace, life and death, of an entire city and all its inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Who were the victims of the sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the citizens of Sarajevo of all ages and of all nationalities were equally the victims of sniping and shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many children were killed or injured by sniping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The total number of people killed was 12,000. 12,000 inhabitants of Sarajevo, killed by sniping and shelling and of that number 1,600 children.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were civilian women particularly in danger of sniping and shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, women had to take over many of the public functions in the city, in medical institutions and all public institutions, and also look after the children a lot more than they used to, so they had to move much more than men and were, therefore, frequent victims of the sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What psychological impact, in your opinion, did the sniping have on the citizens of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very hard. In the beginning, people were simply afraid to go out into the street and especially let children go out to play, even the yards around houses, even if it is protected from sniping, they could have been shelled. But after a certain time, we had to get accustomed to that and life simply went on with sniping and with constant danger of being wounded or killed. Psychologically, the hardest thing was when a mother or a child or a father had to stay out for a long period of time and they had no news of anybody, and their relatives did not know whether he or she was wounded or alive until they came back home, because telephones did not operate, did not work, and any stay outside the house or during a visit to friends or relatives meant fear, panic, about the destiny of the person who was not there within the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: If you unexpectedly had to work late on a particular day, what did you have to do in order to be able to work late and not alarm your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learnt to tell my wife and children, "I will come when I show up", without my usual time when I came back about half past 7 or 10 o'clock in the evening, if something happened in my work after 8 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Sir, were there occasional cease-fires when the sniping would stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were occasional peaceful days and cease-fires which were generated by negotiations or particular resolutions passed by the Security Council, but usually after several days and in 1994 after several months the old situation resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What effect did these broken cease-fires have upon the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The inhabitants of Sarajevo never lost hope and every cease-fire, every improvement in the general situation, raised hopes that peace had finally come. But a return to sniping or the fortification of the blockades and the power failures, the lack of power, water and other services produced a very bad psychological effect, because the worst thing, when you go from a bad situation to an improved situation and then goes back to something that was worse than the previous situation. It was obviously premeditated by those who had put up the siege of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could please have the lights dimmed? We have two photographs to show, Exhibits 155 and 156. Those are numbers 3085 first and then 3086. If we could move to the next photograph, please? Thank you. These photographers depict children who were victims of sniping and shelling. (To the witness): Sir, did the city have adequate medical facilities to treat the victims of the sniping and shelling incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sarajevo had two large hospitals and they operated throughout the war, but from the very beginning they were at the border level, as soon as there was a lack of water, a lack of communication, for 2,000 or more nurses and doctors to go home and come back to work, there were problems. Soon after that the equipment in the hospitals stopped functioning either because of the lack of power or because the generators operated by gas or diesel, there were failures because of technological problems in equipment. Still, because the hospitals served only the city under siege and before the war it used to serve the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina, we, I might say, were lucky as a city as a whole, thanks mostly to the efforts of the doctors and other medical staff, and the fact that the hospital facilities were much greater than was needed for the city itself. Although they were not war hospitals, they were civilian hospitals, and the doctors were trained during the war for sorting out patients and quick treatment of injuries and saving the lives of the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did the citizens of Sarajevo encounter special difficulties in rescuing victims of the shelling and sniping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, a victim -- there was always sniping after a victim and it was a joy to help the wounded, pull him into a car which comes by or which is called to the spot, and be transferred to the hospital or the first aid institution. This usually brought people to that locality which was usually identified as the new target of sniping and shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were there instances of rescuers actually being wounded or killed themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were many instances of that kind. This had a very demoralizing effect on people, but nobody was left in the lurch for a long period of time without a group of people coming to his or her rescue, or at least taking him to a sheltered place, or put him in a car and take him to the hospital. Later, during the war in many parts of the city we developed special centres, emergency centres, where it was easier to bring the wounded to such places so they would not bleed to death, because all the ambulances were destroyed after the first month of the war and the transportation was conducted in ordinary trucks and cars -- anything that was available and could have been used as a transportation means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did the city erect any sort of barricades to protect people in those areas where sniping was frequent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several crossroads intersections in early May were targeted by snipers. During the night, with the help of the UN forces and their organisations, we placed large containers, large commodity containers, or railway carriages for passive resistance, protection from sniping or shells, the smaller calibre shells, that could not go through that, those protection means. All the dangerous intersections were provided with this passive anti-sniping protection. When we ran out of containers, we used ordinary cloth to protect the people walking across the intersections visually, and people usually ran across those intersections to be exposed to that area as little as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could we please have the lights lowered and Exhibits 157 and 158 shown? They would be 3077 and 3078. Thank you. If we could show the next photograph, please? (To the witness): Sir, what do these photographs depict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They depict barricades that were erected with lorries or trollies that had been destroyed, reinforced with concrete elements because the tin itself was not sufficient to protect people from sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were these barricades effective for the people or were there still injuries even in the areas where the barricades existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had an effect, but a small one. Later, we erected more barricades, putting one container on top of another and sometimes they would reach as high as five metres above. That way they became a safe protection, but it was impossible to protect the entire city with these barricades because there were streets and roads that were still exposed to sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: At this point we would like to move to a new topic and that would be the winter of 1992. The winter of 1992 was actually the first winter the people of Sarajevo spent in a state of siege, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Would you just take some time, please, and explain to the court, describe to the court, what that first winter under siege was like, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A large majority of the citizens did not believe in the autumn of 1992 that they would survive the winter without electricity and under a complete siege. The greatest problem was the lack of food and heating. Only about 15 per cent of the city, of the houses and apartments, had gas installed, natural gas, which was used as heating for heating. When towards the end of October 1992 electricity was completely cut off, it was hard to imagine how a city of that size could survive without electricity. Then organised and spontaneous felling of trees began. Paper was collected and special fuel was made from that paper and families gathered in flats where there was natural gas. So several families would live in two or three rooms that had the natural gas infrastructure, because these were heated and could be used also to prepare food. As far as the city authorities are concerned, apart from organising such matters, we were involved in maintaining the large bakery. So, although we did not have electricity, we built generators, gas powered generators, to produce electricity. So, throughout the winter every citizen of Sarajevo could have one-third of a loaf of bread, about 450 grammes, plus the humanitarian aid through UNHCR which was very bad that winter, was inadequate. So it was really hard to make ends meet with the food that was available. That autumn and that winter, I lost 28 kilogrammes and, on the average, every citizen of Sarajevo lost about 25 kilogrammes of body weight, because of the lack of food, food that was very ordinary, very simple, and because of the psychological condition and the insecurity about the end of the winter, survival through the winter. The repairing of the power lines was in charge of the professionals of the international community and the General who was in charge of the Sarajevo UNPROFOR promised electricity by Christmas, after the Catholic Christmas, we thought he meant the Orthodox Christmas which falls in January the following year, but the electricity came only in March 1993, 12 to 15 megawatts, which is less than 10 per cent of the needs of the town, bearing in mind only the housing units, but enough for the functioning, for the operation, of the bakery and for supplying the water and occasional distribution to families. So that a citizen would, on average, have electricity about every third or fourth day just to be able to prepare some food, to watch television for a while and so that children could play their computer games or anything else that was powered by electricity. The marketplace did not function. There was no organised supply of food apart from the humanitarian aid, but on the black market the price of the basic food articles was about 10 or 20 times higher than before the war. For instance, sugar was sold at the price of 80 German Marks; coffee was sold at the price of 120 Marks; matches were a big problem because there were no matches to start a fire. So people would carry a flame so that they could make a fire with what little wood they had, firewood, to cook something or just kill the cold which just permeates the entire building, the entire flat. City transportation was completely out, and I personally remember a picture when people who were going to get water were using sledges and some would use their pets as animals to pull the sledges so it reminded me of a scene from the life of Eskimos. But we manage to survive that winter, too. The hope was that after the winter spring was coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You touched upon it, but could you explain to the court what was done in order to supply the water for the city during the winter of '92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main source for the supply of water to Sarajevo was controlled by Karadzic's Serbs. There was no electricity at the time. There was no water in the distribution system. All the taps were completely dry. The only alternative source of water was old wells of the city brewery. The presidency of the city organised hoses to be placed there so the people could come and fill their vessels with water. The pumps for getting water out of the wells were powered by diesel oil that was provided by the UNHCR. That was the picture of the winter 1992/93. So the people from all parts of the city had to come to the brewery in order to supply themselves with 20 or 25 litres of water, of drinking water. This showed the solidarity among people and the meaning of solidarity because older people were unable to pull those sledges because it is a city, as you saw from the picture, between hills and many people had to go uphill to get the water. But at the same time it was shown how these little things, such as bringing 25 litres of drinking water, meant happiness for a family, because when we have to walk for one or two hours in one direction and then waiting in the queue for a long time and then coming back with drinking water, when the children meet their father, welcome their father, with a happy smile, "Daddy, you have brought water, now we have water for tomorrow too". There was also sniping and shelling and with the help of the UNPROFOR we managed to protect those sources of water, some of the sources of water, from sniping, so that people in the queue would be as safe as possible, although prior to that time many people had been killed in those queues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: As we know, the siege continued to last; was the winter of 1993 any better than the winter of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Psychologically, it was worse because in the winter of 1992 spring was coming, summer was coming, and there was no possibility to live through another year of -- winter of siege. So, that winter and especially during the summer, the improvised natural gas system was widened because it was the natural gas that really saved the city in 1992. This also brought danger in terms of possibilities of explosion of gas, and now there was not enough gas because a lot was lost in these improvised systems and also the supplier of the natural gas, the Russian Federation, was not really disposed to increase the amount of the gas because they were not paid. There was firewood in the city, but in terms of climate, it was a milder winter and was objectively easier psychologically; nevertheless, it was more difficult because it was a repeat of what happened during the first winter of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we will move into just some of the general conditions of life during the entire siege and cover a few of the more critical aspects. Throughout the entire siege who controlled the electricity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sarajevo had a very modern system of supply of electricity. Eleven transformer stations around the city enabled triple security for a maximum consumption of electricity during the Olympic Games. All these transformer stations were controlled first by the JNA and then later also by the army of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Had the JNA secured the important power sites for electricity before the fighting actually began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they simply captured those transformer stations and later they became the army of the Bosnian Serbs. That army kept control of those transformer stations all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could you describe to the court what it is like to be in a large city at night without any electricity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once as the town Mayor I happened to be in Vienna when at the airport there was an electricity failure for a couple of minutes. Of course there was an alternative system but the air-conditioning could not work. You can imagine what it means within a system which must have a power supply when that power ceases. The elevators do not work. The water cannot reach higher than the fifth floor because the water pumps are not operating for supplying from the upper floors. The city transport is not working. You have some batteries for listening to the radio, then you run out of batteries. There are no possibilities for accumulating power. In the autumn of '92 when the electricity was cut for the first time, it was hard to imagine that life could be organised without power, no telephones, special phones or anything, no telephones or anything, the Town Mayor or anyone, because no generators were operating. They worked for a day or two and then they stopped. But after that shock one realises that life has to be organised even under such conditions and then, somehow, one survives. Some alternative generator is found. We would pull out our engines from our motor cars, and then we would make small generators for power production to fill in the accumulations or to be able to satisfy our priorities for power. We managed afterwards to bring in several generators as gifts with the help of UNPROFOR or the International Red Cross. As I already said, these bakeries and the brewery with water pumps, they had a constant supply of power for 10 or 12 hours which was the minimum requirement for them to be able to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did Karadzic's Serbs sometimes allow electricity and water to come back into the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they would always say that they would no longer use these essential needs for the life of the city for military purposes, that they would no longer cut the electricity supply or the gas supply or close the valves for the transport of water. Indeed, occasionally for a month or two the situation was improved considerably. For instance, every day households would have electricity for six hours and every other day they would get water for an hour or two. This was an enormous improvement and people thought that an improvement was coming and the situation would be normalized, but again after a month or two, whatever the occasion may have been, there was a complete stop and this was a psychological blow for us as people. This oscillation between zero and the minimum state of the infrastructure was a tactic which was meant to provoke among people a feeling of hopelessness of continuing life in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that Sarajevo was proud of its transportation system. When the siege began what happened to the tram system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The trams were the pride of the city, because Sarajevo was the first in central Europe to acquire tram transportation 130 years ago. First it was horse drawn and then electric trams. The city transport functioned very well because the city was stretched out about 13 kilometres from one end to the other. That was the longest tram line. As of May 2nd the trams came to a halt completely and after a lull in the course of '94 they resumed service, but there were frequent interruptions because of sniping or because of shelling attacks on trams. For many citizens the sound of the tram bells in the morning at 6.30 or 7 a.m. were a sign that the day would probably be a quiet one, because as soon as the trams started working one could go to work. There were no night operations anywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina to warrant shelling of the city and prevent the trams from working. So that in a way for the citizens of Sarajevo as well as for those who were attacking the city, they were a symbol of the city. That is why they were frequently a target of attack by snipers or shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: As you mentioned there were children within the city during the siege. How did the city handle the educational needs of the children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first it was very hard because after a few days underground or in apartments children wanted to go out, and their parents could not allow them to do that because it was very dangerous. That is when private schools started or actually children from several apartments would get together in a teacher's home or a mother who had talent to amuse children for a time and to organise a game or some form of instruction. With time we managed to mobilize schools somewhere in the early spring of '93 and all children were encompassed by schools that were not organised in actual school buildings, but in basements, in apartments or any other suitable buildings that were safe from sniping and shelling. As there was no electricity, there were several shifts of two or three hours each, so that the children had a feeling of going to school and were given homework to do with their parents, so as to cover the necessary curriculum somehow. With time this organisation of schools was improved, text books were printed in Slovenia and transported to Bosnia and distributed among school children. Many humanitarian organisations assisted, so that the children for those four academic years did not waste them altogether. They did manage to learn quite a lot, but I think they learnt most about the life that was imposed upon them. The time is now coming when the gaps in their education need to be filled, and this is a whole generation, four years of schooling regardless of the level, which has been deprived of a normal education, but it is still fortunate to have survived and to be able to continue a normal education as of this academic year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Sir, you have children that remained with you during the siege. How old were they when the siege started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My son was 11 and my daughter 8 when the siege began. They spent the whole time with me and my wife in Sarajevo, together with some other 50,000 children of Sarajevo who spent all the time of the war in Sarajevo. That is roughly about one half of the total number of school aged children that we had in Sarajevo before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: In your opinion, how did the siege affect daily family life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Daily family life was simply totally changed during the siege. Children could not go out to play. They could not go to school, and what is important for the life of a family is that children had to be amused somehow, kept busy, because children are very sensitive when they do not know what to do. As there was no electricity then all kinds of games, card games, chess and other games for which electricity is not necessary were popular. However, in the evening when it got dark you could use a candle for a short time because, especially in the first winter and the second too, there was a shortage of candles or any other lighting systems. The winter nights are very long if you go to bed at 7 or 8 o'clock, maybe one or two hours after total darkness fell, and if it is a peaceful night one would spend it in a half sleep having psychological problems because the night is too long. Then the next day he is happy. If it is a foggy day, because there will be no sniping even if it is overcast, at least it is an occasion to see friends, shall we say, or organise something for the next day when the danger will be increased for movement in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How did the siege affect the daily lives of the women who were trapped in the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The women who were working, who were employed either in companies or in the public services, had to move daily from their apartments to their place of work. They had an extra obligation, that is, to appear to be decently clothed, clean, with the minimum of makeup they had left to retain the dignity of women, and those who stayed at home with their families, their children or elderly parents also had additional obligations to maintain the family, to preserve the family because, after all, life somehow focused on the woman of the family who stayed at home. It was very hard to take care of children, to worry about food or one's husband, to worry whether he will come home alive and to keep in touch, but I think that the women of Sarajevo managed and made a crucial contribution to the survival of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Were there special problems associated with caring for the elderly that remained in the city during the siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many elderly people were alone, and for their most essential needs we organised segments of the civil protection or the young men and women who were not on duty to supply them with water, to bring them food, to provide medical care for the elderly, to respond to Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 359 to 365. their complaints when they were not feeling well, because older people under such circumstances could hardly go out. They simply could not run across a street that was exposed to sniping. So they would not go out at all, or if they were living on the sixth floor, the seventh floor, if they go down and there is no lift operating they cannot get back. So that older people did not leave their apartments for months on end. Then we would organise through these local medical institutions visits to these elderly people when they would take their blood pressure, do the necessary medical check-ups every few months or every few weeks for the ailing, to provide preventative care against other diseases which, due to malnutrition and the poor quality of the treatment, the risk of such diseases was increased during the siege. Many elderly people died, not from shelling or sniping, but simply because the medical protection under those conditions declined. They died of natural causes, but certainly many of them much sooner than they would have done if it had not been for such conditions. Therefore, in addition to these 12,000 victims of sniping and shelling, 4,500 people died of natural causes, but even that "natural" should be in quotation marks because certainly they would have lived longer under normal conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did the citizens of Sarajevo encounter any difficulties with burying the dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the ugliest, the darkest things because to bury one's dead -- the burial of dead was also a target of sniping and shelling. Many people would get wounded and then we would postpone to night time the funerals or special places where we organised temporary cemeteries to protect the participants attending such funeral rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Could we have the lights lowered, please, and if we could have Exhibit 159, 3081, shown on the screen, please? Sir, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is a small cemetery next to a garage made of concrete. You can see parts of the fence of that garage which provided some protection from sniping and shelling. To the right is a park which is exposed to sniping and which throughout the period from the beginning of the siege served also for local farming. So that on the same spot were remnants of this large garage, a cemetery for 30 or 40 people buried during the night or early in the morning when one expected it would be peaceful, and at night at 10 or 20 metres from this spot onions were raised or other vegetables for elementary survival. This is in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of what happened when people actually tried to bury people in this particular narrow plot of land?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, once the funeral was at 10 p.m. and just as the people had got together they started firing from several hundred metres away, the barracks, Karadzic's Serbs started firing. Then people ran away and the body was left there, and then after midnight they came back to complete the burial ceremony. Later on these burials were carried out at 2 after midnight, at 2 o'clock in the morning, a very strange time but the safest for 50 or 100 people that could come to pay their last respects to a neighbour or relative who had been killed. Of course, these are all mixed inhabitants, and there are both Orthodox and Catholic tombs lying one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. When did the refugees first start coming to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first refugees started coming in April 1992 from the small villages or suburbs of Sarajevo where they were the victims of so-called ethnic cleansing by the Serbs. So they came either into the centre of the city or some went elsewhere to the other side of the siege towards central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did the influx of refugees create additional problems for the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, the refugees came to Sarajevo not because they wanted to be refugees or because they wanted to come to Sarajevo, because the conditions of life in Sarajevo were such that it was no good for the inhabitants and still worse for refugees coming without anything, and often bringing a wounded member of the family with them. However, that too was a way to survive. Most of the refugees came from eastern Bosnia, from Foca, Rogatica, Visegrad and other localities a lot closer to Serbia and also from eastern Herzegovina, from parts which were ethnically cleansed of all non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When did the siege finally end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The siege ended in mid-March this year, when Ilidza was reintegrated, when the road from Sarajevo towards Mostar and Tuzla was opened, that is towards the outside world.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: So how long did the entire siege last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somebody used the 5th or 6th April as the date of the beginning of the siege when the fighting started, but that siege was not as yet complete. It was complete as of May 2nd 1992, because until May 2nd the last bus and the last local train left Sarajevo from the Sarajevo railway station to a nearby station. So that from May 1992 until March '96, almost four years, that was the duration of the siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Sir, in your opinion did the political and military leaders of Karadzic's Serbs know what was happening to the civilians in Sarajevo as a result of the siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What is the basis for your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tactics of besieging Sarajevo was adjusted on the one hand to the international situation, the pressure brought to bear on them by the international community, and on the other side to the situation in the city. This stifling of the city was constantly -- there was a dosage. It was greater or lesser so as to show during those four years that the city was under the full control and left at the mercy of the army of Karadzic's Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, it would be impossible, and indeed presumptuous of the Prosecutor's Office, to attempt to truly recreate what daily life was in Sarajevo, but what we have done is we have put together a brief montage collection of some of the video clips, film clips we have collected as evidence. With the Court's permission, we would like to end the day with showing that montage of life in Sarajevo. If we could have the lights dimmed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Perhaps, counsel, we could just briefly see how we are going to proceed. I do not know what your plans are in terms of the Mayor of Sarajevo. Could he stay till tomorrow morning because it is now 5.30 and you are going to show us this montage and thereafter I assume my fellow Judges and myself would like to put a number of questions to the witness? Can the witness remain without any difficulties in The Hague this evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Absolutely, your Honour. We have made provisions for that. We could have questions tomorrow with any follow-up that the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Well, on that understanding then, I think we are going to adjourn and we shall resume tomorrow morning at 10 o'clock. Thank you very much. (5.30 p.m.)

procedural_notes.text: (The hearing adjourned until the following day)
